passages.title: The clear Book and the deniers' coming regret
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat set two things beside each other: a revelation described as plain and clear (ayah 1), and people who will one day wish, with everything in them, that they had been Muslims (ayah 2). Between those two statements sits an obvious question — if that is how it ends, why are the deniers still eating, still comfortable, still making plans? Ayat 3–5 speak to exactly that. Their ease is not approval, and the delay is not safety: every township has a decree already known.

## Ayah 1 — "These are the verses of the Book"

The surah opens with the disconnected letters **Alif–Lām–Rā**. Ibn Kathir does not pause over them here; he simply notes that he has already discussed the letters that open some surahs, and moves straight on to what follows. That restraint is worth imitating. Curiosity about the letters is natural, but the weight of this opening lies in the claim made immediately after them.

That claim is about the revelation itself. The ayah calls it *the Book*, and then *a clear Qur'an* — Ibn Kathir's rendering is "a plain Qur'an" (the Arabic word is *mubīn*). Before any argument with the deniers begins, the first thing said about this revelation is that it is plain. Whatever difficulty a reader meets later, the surah does not open by presenting its message as obscure.

## Ayah 2 — the wish that comes too late

**"How much would those who disbelieved wish that they had been Muslims."** Ibn Kathir states the meaning plainly: "they will regret having lived in disbelief, and will wish that they had been Muslims in this world."

Notice the shape of the regret. It is not a wish to be spared, and not a wish that the Fire were less severe. It is a wish about a life already spent — that they had lived it differently. Regret in this ayah is aimed backwards, at a door that has closed. Notice too that neither rendering in front of us leaves the wish faint or occasional: "how much would those who disbelieved wish," and, in the translation used here, they "will certainly wish."

Ibn Kathir does not leave the timing vague. He records two early explanations that fix the exact moment this wish erupts.

**First**, Sufyan Ath-Thawri reported from Salamah bin Kuhayl, from Abi Az-Za'ra', from 'Abdullah, who said this is about *the Jahannamiyyun* — the sinners among the believers who will stay in Hell for some time — at the moment when the disbelievers **see them being brought out of Hell**.

**Second**, Ibn Jarir reported that Ibn 'Abbas and Anas bin Malik explained the ayah as referring to the Day when Allah will detain the sinful Muslims in Hell along with the idolaters. The idolaters say to them: "What you used to worship on earth has not helped you." Then, by virtue of His mercy, Allah will be angry for their sake, and He will remove them from it. *That* is the moment the ayah describes.

Read those two reports together and the scene becomes almost unbearable in its irony. The mockery comes first — the idolaters jeer at believers who are suffering, as though the matter were settled and faith had proved worthless. And it is exactly then that the ones being mocked are lifted out, while the mockers remain, watching, and finally understand what it would have meant to have been Muslims. The wish of ayah 2 is the wish of someone who sees clearly at the one moment when seeing clearly can change nothing.

One point of belief in these reports deserves to be said out loud, because it is easy to miss: a believer weighed down by sin may be detained in the Fire and yet be brought out of it. That is what the term *Jahannamiyyun* in Ibn Kathir's report refers to, and it is why faith is never a small thing, however heavy the sins that accompany it. Observe also what Allah's anger in the second report is *for*: it is anger on behalf of those believers, and the report ties it to His mercy — "by virtue of His mercy, Allah will be angry for their sake, and He will remove them."

## Ayah 3 — "Leave them"

**"Leave them to eat and enjoy, and let them be preoccupied with (false) hope. They will come to know!"**

This sounds at first like Allah turning away in indifference. Ibn Kathir corrects that at once: it is "a stern and definitive threat." He places it beside two other ayat where the same permission is granted in the same tone — *"Enjoy your brief life! But certainly, your destination is the Fire!"* (14:30), and *"Eat and enjoy yourselves for a little while. Verily, you are the guilty."* (77:46). In each, the pleasure is handed over precisely because it is short and because it ends somewhere. To be left alone with your appetites, unchecked, is not a mercy. It is a sentence being carried out slowly.

Three things fill the disbelievers' horizon in this ayah: eating, enjoying, and being diverted by *al-amal* — hope, expectation, the long project stretching out ahead. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurtubi, glosses this phrase as "the making of long-drawn plans with engrossing love, and the greed for the material without any concern for death and 'Akhirah" — the *Ākhirah* being the life to come, the accounting of deeds there, and the reward and punishment that follow. So it is not planning as such; it is planning that has swallowed the planner.

And Ibn Kathir supplies the exact damage such hope does: it leaves them "distracted from repentance and turning to Allah." That is the measure of dangerous hope — not how ambitious it is, but what it crowds out. A plan that leaves no room in the heart for turning back to Allah has already cost more than it can earn.

The ayah closes: **"They will soon come to know!"** — which Ibn Kathir explains as knowing "their punishment." The knowledge does arrive. It simply arrives as experience rather than as warning, and by then it is the knowledge of ayah 2, useful for nothing but regret.

### What this does *not* condemn

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful here, and the care matters, because this ayah is easy to misapply. It says that making eating and drinking the real occupation and aim of life, keeping glued to long-drawn material plans while surrounded by countless comforts, and becoming totally heedless of death, is something that can be done only by the disbelievers — the reason being that they do not believe in the *Ākhirah*, the accounting of deeds there, and the reward and punishment for it.

A believer, it says plainly, eats and drinks too. He takes care of his economic needs to the measure of necessity. He makes future plans for his occupation and business. The difference is not that he abstains from living; it is that he does none of it by forgetting death and ignoring his concern for the *Ākhirah*. So he is careful about what he does and finds out whether it is *halal* or *haram* — permissible or forbidden. And he does not occupy himself with wasteful or unnecessary plans and projections, whether as a hobby or out of compulsion.

Maʿārif also makes an explicit exemption: plans made to achieve religious objectives, or made to guard the future interests of a people or a country, are **not** included in what the ayah criticises — because that kind of planning is itself a form of concern for the *Ākhirah*.

### From the Sunnah and the early generations

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān brings a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ, cited by Qurtubi from *Musnad al-Bazzar* on the authority of Sayyidna Anas, may Allah be pleased with him: four things are signs of being unfortunate — (1) not being able to shed tears, that is, not being in tears when ashamed of acts of negligence and sin; (2) hard-heartedness; (3) fanciful hopes and plans for the future; and (4) greed for worldly things. It is worth sitting with the company those four keep. Runaway hopes and greed appear in the same list as a dry eye and a hard heart. They are not separate ailments; the list treats them as symptoms of one condition.

Maʿārif also reports the Prophet ﷺ as saying that the first set of people from this Ummah — this community of believers — will have their salvation because of their perfect faith and their avoidance of the pursuit of the material, the *dunya*; and the later people of the Ummah will be destroyed because of miserliness and fancies projected too far. (The commentary quotes this without naming a collection, so take it as the teaching it conveys.)

Then there is Sayyidna Abu Ad-Darda', may Allah be pleased with him, who stood up on the pulpit of the congregational mosque of Damascus and asked the people to listen to a brother who wished them well. There were big people before you, he told them — they made big money, collected gold and things, built magnificent palaces, and made long-hauled plans and projections for the future. Today they are dust; their residences are their graves; and all those long-winded hopes and plans have proved to be no more than a web of deception. He reminded them that close to them had lived the people of 'Ad, who had stuffed their country with fighting men, wealth, means, possessions, arms and horses. Then he asked whether anyone present would buy what they left behind as their legacy — for two silver dirhams.

And Imam Al-Hasan Al-Basri, as Al-Qurtubi records, put it in a single line: a person with long plans, hopes and fancies is bound to ruin his proper conduct in life. The point is not that the future is unknowable. It is that a heart fixed on a horizon it will never reach stops doing well the thing in front of it today.

## Ayat 4–5 — the term nobody can move

**"And never did We destroy a township but there was a known decree for it. No nation can advance its term, nor delay it."**

These two ayat answer the question that ayah 3 leaves hanging. If they are so plainly wrong, why are they still prospering? Ibn Kathir gives the answer in two conditions: Allah "never destroys a township until He has established evidences for it and its allotted time has ended." Both must be satisfied. The evidences must be established, and the appointed moment must arrive.

Then ayah 5 closes both doors at once. Ibn Kathir: "When the time for a nation's destruction has come, He never delays it, and He never moves its appointed time forward." A people can neither hurry their term nor push it back an hour. So the one who reads delay as acquittal has misread it: the clock is running on a schedule he cannot see and cannot touch. And the one who reads delay as neglect has misread it just as badly.

Ibn Kathir names the immediate audience: this was "a message and a warning to the people of Makkah, telling them to give up their *Shirk*" — setting up others alongside Allah in worship — "their stubbornness and disbelief for which they deserved to be destroyed." That the warning was issued at all tells you where they stood: still able to hear it, still able to act on it. A warning is only worth giving while there is still time.

## Living it

- **Take the clarity at face value.** Ayah 1 calls this revelation a plain Qur'an. Treating it as a locked puzzle meant for specialists is not humility; the opening claim is that it is plain, and a plain thing asks to be picked up.
- **Audit what your planning displaces.** Ibn Kathir's test is precise: does this hope leave room for repentance and turning to Allah, or has it quietly taken that room? Ambition is not the problem; the crowding-out is.
- **Keep the two questions Maʿārif gives you.** Is this halal or haram? And is this plan necessary, or a projection I have taken up as a hobby or a compulsion? Plans for the sake of your religion, or to guard the future interests of your people or country, pass that test by design.
- **Never read a delay as a verdict.** Neither your own unpunished sins nor another's untroubled prosperity tells you how the account stands. Ayah 5 is explicit that timing is fixed by Allah, not earned by the one enjoying it.
- **Let ayah 2 do its work now.** The regret it describes is available today at no cost, and on that Day at every cost. The point of being told in advance what the deniers will wish is that you can wish it while wishing still changes something.

passages.title: "You are possessed!" and the guarded Reminder
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** Here the deniers of Makkah speak in their own voice: they call the Prophet ﷺ mad, and they demand that angels be produced as proof. Allah answers not by defending the sanity of His Prophet ﷺ, but by telling them what would actually happen if angels came — and then by putting His own name behind the Book they were sneering at.

What holds the four ayat together is a single word: **al-Dhikr**, "the Reminder", which is a name of the Qur'an. They throw it at him in ayah 6 — "O you to whom the *Reminder* has been sent down!" — and in ayah 9 Allah takes the very same word back into His own speech: *Verily, We, it is We Who revealed the Dhikr — the Qur'an — and surely We will guard it.* Their mockery is answered with a guarantee.

## Ayah 6: mockery dressed up as an address

Look at how they build the sentence. They do not say "Muhammad". They address him by the claim itself: *O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down.* Ibn Kathir reads the phrase exactly as it was meant — it means, in their mouths, "the one who **claims** to receive it." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān supplies the same silent parenthesis when it paraphrases their words: "O you to whom the Qur'an has been revealed, **(as you claim)**…" It is the tone of a man who quotes your title back at you in order to laugh at it.

Then comes the charge: *Verily, you are a madman.* Maulana Ashraf ʿAli Thanavi, quoted in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, unfolds what they were really saying: "you are certainly — Allah forbid — insane **(and your claim to prophethood is false, otherwise)** why would you not bring the angels to us…" The insult and the demand are one move. Calling him mad is how they justify refusing him.

Why madness, of all charges? Ibn Kathir gives the reason plainly: they meant he was mad **"by your invitation to us to follow you and leave the way of our forefathers."** The accusation is not medical, it is social. In a society where the fathers' path is the measure of sanity, the one man who will not be moved by that consensus must be the one who has lost his mind. Ibn Kathir sums up what their speech reveals: "the disbelief, arrogance and stubbornness of the disbelievers."

## Ayah 7: "Bring us the angels, if you are truthful"

Their second move sounds far more reasonable than the first. Ibn Kathir explains what they were asking for: angels brought down **"to bear witness to the accuracy of what you have brought to us"** — a heavenly delegation to confirm the messenger's credentials. Thanavi renders their demand the same way: angels "who will testify your truthfulness before us."

But the Qur'an files this demand under a known genre, and both commentaries point that out by lining it up with other ayat. Pharaoh said of Musa, *"Why then are not golden bracelets bestowed on him, or angels sent along with him?"* (43:53). Maʿārif cites the parallel in Surah al-Furqan, *"Why is not an angel sent down unto him, to be a warner with him?"* (25:7). And Ibn Kathir quotes the passage in which Allah passes judgement on this whole way of speaking: *"And those who do not expect a meeting with Us say: 'Why are not the angels sent down to us, or why do we not see our Lord?' Indeed they think too highly of themselves, and are scornful with great pride"* (25:21).

That is the verdict: not honest inquiry but arrogance. And note who is quoted saying it — "those who do not expect a meeting with Us", whom Ibn Kathir identifies as "those who deny the Day of Resurrection and the life of the Hereafter." The demand for angels grows out of not really believing in the Hereafter at all.

There is also a grim mercy in how that same passage continues: *"On the Day that they do see the angels — there will be no good news given on that day to the guilty. And they (angels) will say: 'All kinds of glad tidings are forbidden for you'"* (25:22). They will get their angels. They will get them on the one day when the sight brings no comfort at all.

## Ayah 8: the answer — and the mercy hidden inside it

Allah replies in two clauses, and each one dismantles half of the demand.

**"We do not send the angels down except with the truth."** Thanavi, quoted in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, renders it: "We send down the angels **(in the manner asked by them) only to enforce a decision**." The descent they were calling for is not a display arranged to settle an argument; it is the carrying out of a verdict.

What does *bi'l-ḥaqq*, "with the truth", mean here? The commentaries record a genuine difference:

- **Mujahid**, cited by Ibn Kathir, said it means "with the Message and the punishment" — the two errands on which angels are sent down.
- **Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** reports that *al-ḥaqq* here means the decision to send down punishment, while some commentators take it to denote the Qur'an, or prophethood. Bayan al-Qur'an gives preference to the first meaning, which is reported from **al-Hasan al-Basri**.

Mujahid's reading holds both strands together; the reading Bayan al-Qur'an prefers is the one the second half of the ayah then explains.

**"And in that case, they would have no respite."** No delay, no stay of execution. Thanavi spells out the logic: had the angels come down exactly as demanded and these people still did not believe — "as their ways guarantee" — they "would have been destroyed instantly"; and he points the reader to Surah al-Anʿam (6:8–9), where the reason for this has already been given.

So read the answer again. It is not only a rebuke; it is a reprieve. They asked for the one thing that would have finished them, and they were given time instead. Every morning the sky did not open over Makkah was another morning in which someone among them could still change his mind. The refusal *was* the mercy.

## Ayah 9: "and surely We will guard it"

Now the Reminder they mocked in ayah 6 returns, and this time Allah is the speaker: *Verily, We, it is We Who revealed the Dhikr — the Qur'an — and surely We will guard it from corruption.* Ibn Kathir states the sense simply: Allah **"is the One Who revealed the Dhikr to him, which is the Qur'an, and He is protecting it from being changed or altered."**

The whole exchange has been turned inside out. The ayah does not argue about the man they insulted; it speaks about the Book and about the One Who sent it down and keeps it safe.

## The scribe in al-Ma'mun's court

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates an incident which Imam al-Qurtubi reports as authentic, and it is the best illustration of this ayah at work in the world.

The Abbasid Khalifah al-Ma'mun used to host debates on intellectual questions at his court, where scholars of every kind were welcome. A Jewish man attended one of them — elegant in looks, dress and manners, and eloquent and intellectually bright in the debate itself. Afterwards al-Ma'mun called him over, confirmed that he was an Israelite, and invited him to Islam, telling him he could hope for the best possible treatment. He answered that he was not willing to leave the religion of his forefathers. The matter ended there, and he left.

A year later the same man was back — as a Muslim, and making a very distinct contribution to the court's discussion of Islamic jurisprudence. Afterwards al-Ma'mun called him aside again and asked what had made him accept Islam.

He said: when I went back from here, I decided to do some research on the religions of the day. I am a scribe; I write books and sell them, and they bring a good price. So I made a test. First I calligraphed three manuscripts of the Torah, making additions and deletions of my own. I took them to the synagogue, and the Jews found them interesting and bought them. Then I did the same with the Injil — three manuscripts, complete with my additions and deletions — and took them to the church, and the Christians were pleased with them and bought them. After that I tried the same thing with the Qur'an. I calligraphed three good-looking manuscripts, of course with the usual additions and deletions of my own. When I went out to sell them, I faced a problem. Every buyer I went to would take the manuscript, look into it to determine whether it was correct or not, and when he noticed the additions or deletions, he would quietly hand it back to me.

"From this episode," he said, "I learnt my lesson that this Book is protected, and protected by Allah Taʿala Himself — therefore I embraced Islam."

**The reason why.** Qadi Yahya ibn Aktham, who narrates the incident, performed Hajj that same year and told the story to Sufyan ibn ʿUyainah. Sufyan replied that surely this is how it should be, because it is confirmed by the Qur'an. When the Qur'an mentions the Torah and the Injil, it says that the Jews and the Christians "have been entrusted with the responsibility of protecting" those Books of Allah (5:44). This is why, when they did not fulfil that duty, the Books were lost through distortions and alterations. Of this Book, Allah said instead: *"And We are there to protect it."*

That is a precise point, and worth holding on to: the difference the narration draws is in who was made responsible for the guarding. With the earlier Books, that duty was placed on the people who received them; with this Book, Allah Taʿala Himself arranged to have it remain protected — and so, despite thousands of efforts by its enemies, not a single change in one tiny dot or case mark could be made.

**And it is still visible.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what this looks like today: more than fourteen hundred years have passed since the blessed age of the Prophet ﷺ, and there has been shortfall and neglect on the part of Muslims in all areas of their religious matters — yet the continuous worldwide arrangement of memorising the Qur'an stands as firmly established as it was. In every period of time there are millions of Muslims, old and young, male and female, in whose hearts and minds the Qur'an lives protected. Before them, not even the highest of the high religious scholars can dare recite a single letter wrongly, because among those present — seniors or children — many would promptly catch the error.

## What exactly is under guard: the words *and* the meanings

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds an argument here that is easy to miss and very consequential.

As a matter of principle, it says, all learned people agree that "the Qur'an" is not a name for its words alone, nor for its meanings alone, but for both together. The proof is on both sides. Qur'anic meanings and subjects appear in other books too — the subjects of Islamic writings are essentially Qur'anic — yet nobody calls those books the Qur'an, because they are not its words. And if someone borrowed words and sentences from the Qur'an and wrote an article out of them, no one would call that the Qur'an either, even though nothing in it came from outside. The Qur'an is the exclusive name of that one Divinely revealed Book whose words and meanings are simultaneously protected.

**A ruling that follows.** On this basis Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states that the practice of publishing a translation of the Qur'an in a foreign language and giving it the name "an English Qur'an" or "an Urdu Qur'an" is not permissible at all — because that is not the Qur'an.

**And a second consequence: the Sunnah.** If the protection Allah took upon Himself covers the meanings and not only the words, then it covers the way those meanings were taught. The one sent to teach them was the Prophet ﷺ: *"that you may explain to people what has been sent down to them"* (16:44), and *"He teaches them the Book and the Wisdom"* (3:164). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also records his own words about his mission — "As for me, I have been sent as a teacher" (the commentary quotes this without naming a collection). His medium of instruction to his community was a set of his sayings and doings; and that set of words and deeds is what is known as the Hadith. Hence the conclusion Maʿārif draws in the strongest terms: *"One who says that the Ahadith of the Rasul ﷺ of Allah are not absolutely protected is really saying that the Qur'an is not protected."*

To the familiar objection — that the treasure of Ahadith in the authentic books cannot be trusted because it was documented much later than the blessed age of the Prophet ﷺ — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers on two levels. First, the assumption itself is not correct: the process of protecting and documenting Hadith had already started within the age of prophethood itself, though it was completed later. Second, the Hadith of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ *is* the explanation of the Qur'an and the meaning of the Qur'an, and that protection is something Allah Taʿala has taken upon Himself. How could it be that only the words of the Qur'an remain protected while the meanings go to waste?

## Living it

**When your faith is called madness, do not take the bait.** Notice that ayat 8 and 9 do not argue about the sanity of the Prophet ﷺ at all. The reply lifts the subject away from him entirely and rests it on Allah — who sends the angels, and who guards the Book. That is where a believer's composure can come from when the same charge is made in modern words.

**Do not set the terms of the proof.** The demand of ayah 7 sounds like a fair request for evidence, and ayah 8 shows what it really was — and what it would have cost them. When we catch ourselves saying "if Allah would only show me *this*, I would be certain," the honest question is whether we have weighed the evidence already in our hands: the Reminder itself.

**Read delay as mercy.** *"They would have no respite"* implies that the time we are living in is itself a gift held open. The person still able to repent today has what Quraysh unknowingly asked to have taken away.

**Hold the guarded Book.** Ayah 9 is the reason the copy of the Qur'an in your hands can be trusted letter for letter, and the reason a child who has memorised it can catch a senior scholar's slip. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to that living, worldwide chain of memorisation as the visible face of Allah's protection — and every portion any of us commits to memory is a small place in it.

passages.title: Every messenger was mocked, and no sign would convince them
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat are a word of steadying comfort to the Prophet ﷺ in the face of the Quraysh's rejection — and, in the same breath, an X-ray of the heart that mocks. What holds them together is a single claim, followed all the way down: the rejection he was meeting was not new, not personal, and not caused by any shortage of evidence. Ayat 10–11 place his experience inside a long line of prophets. Ayah 12 explains what is actually happening inside the mockers. Ayah 13 points to the well-known record of everyone who did this before. And ayat 14–15 close the argument with a supposition that removes the last excuse: even a gate opened in the sky would not have moved them.

## The consolation underneath the words

Ibn Kathir opens his comment on this passage by naming its purpose plainly: Allah is **consoling His Messenger ﷺ for the rejection of the disbelieving Quraysh**. He tells him that He sent Messengers before him to the nations of the past, and that **no Messenger came to a nation but they rejected him and mocked him**.

That is the emotional centre of ayah 10 and ayah 11. Notice how the Qur'an comforts. It does not tell the Prophet ﷺ that the ridicule does not sting, and it does not promise him that it will stop tomorrow. It widens the frame. *This has happened to every man who ever stood where you are standing.* The pain is real; what is removed is the private, isolating thought that something has gone uniquely wrong with this mission.

The wording of ayah 11 sharpens it. It is not a report about one particular nation on one particular day; it is open-ended — *no messenger comes to them except that they are mocking him*. Ibn Kathir reads it exactly so: no Messenger came to a nation but they rejected him and mocked him. Ibn Kathir even titles the section **"The Idolators of Every Nation made a Mockery of their Messengers."** Ridicule is presented as the standard reception a messenger met.

## "Among the groups of earlier peoples" — the language of ayah 10

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives a lexical note here that repays slow reading.

The word **اَلشِيَعِ** in ayah 10 is the plural form of **شِیعہ** — the source transliterates it as *shah* — which means the follower or helper of a person. The word is then also used to denote a group that agrees upon particular beliefs and theoretical assumptions. So the sense of the statement is that Allah has sent messengers among *every* group or sect — not to one favoured civilisation while the rest of humanity was left in the dark.

Then the finer point. The ayah says the messengers were sent **فِي شِيَعِ الْأَوَّلِينَ**, using **فِی** — *in / among* the groups of the earlier peoples — and not **اِلٰی** (*ila*), *to* them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws two implications from that single preposition:

- The messenger for every group was **sent from among that particular group**, so that people would find it easy to trust him.
- And because he was one of them, he was **aware of their taste and temperament**, and could therefore make appropriate plans to work for their reform.

This is a quiet mercy hidden in a preposition. Allah did not merely deliver a message; He delivered it through someone the people already knew, fitted to who they were. Which makes the mockery in ayah 11 all the more striking: they were not rejecting an alien intruder. They were rejecting one of their own.

## What is let into the heart (ayah 12)

**كَذَٰلِكَ نَسْلُكُهُ فِي قُلُوبِ الْمُجْرِمِينَ** — "Thus We allow it to enter the hearts of the guilty."

Two questions matter here: what is the "it", and who are "the guilty"?

**The "it".** Ibn Kathir explains the ayah as Allah telling His Prophet ﷺ that **He lets disbelief enter the hearts of those sinners**. He then reports that **Anas and Al-Hasan Al-Basri** said this referred to **Shirk** — associating partners with Allah. So what is being made to enter is not confusion or bad luck; it is the specific disease of denial and idolatry settling into a chest and making itself at home.

It is worth pausing on how the pronouns shift between ayah 12 and ayah 13. In ayah 12, "it" is the disbelief that enters. In ayah 13, **لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِهِ** — "They would not believe in it" — the "it" is, as Ibn Kathir's rendering makes explicit, **the Qur'an**. One thing enters and takes root; the other is kept out. A heart already occupied has no room left for the revelation.

**The "guilty" — al-mujrimīn.** The translation renders the word as "the guilty"; Ibn Kathir speaks of them as "those sinners". His wording is careful about *which* sinners: Allah lets disbelief enter the hearts of **those sinners who are too stubborn and too arrogant to follow His guidance**. The description comes first. It is into *such* hearts that disbelief is made to enter.

Hold both halves of the ayah as they were given. The ayah states openly that it is **He** who allows this to enter — that is the plain wording, and we take it as it came. And in the very same breath the passage supplies the human portrait: mockery in ayah 11, and arrogance and stubbornness in Ibn Kathir's description in ayah 12. Nothing here is presented as a misfortune that fell upon people who were listening humbly.

## "The example of the ancients has already gone forth" (ayah 13)

**وَقَدْ خَلَتْ سُنَّةُ الْأَوَّلِينَ** is rendered "and already the example of the ancients has gone forth" — a precedent already laid down and already run through. Ibn Kathir explains it as: **the destruction wrought by Allah on those who rejected His Messengers, and how He saved His Prophets and their followers in this world and in the Hereafter, is well known.**

Read that twice, because it has two halves and most people only hear the first.

The warning half is aimed at the rejecters: what happened to earlier peoples who rejected their Messengers is not a secret — Ibn Kathir's word is "well known". And the precedent has *already gone forth*. You are not being threatened with something unprecedented; you are being invited to look at the record.

The second half is aimed at the Prophet ﷺ and everyone standing with him: the same well-known record includes Allah **saving** His Prophets and their followers — and Ibn Kathir specifies, in this world *and* in the Hereafter. The pattern that destroys the mocker is the same pattern that rescues the mocked. If history is a warning to one side, it is a promise to the other.

## The gate in the sky (ayat 14–15)

Now comes the passage's most striking image. Ibn Kathir introduces it under the heading: *The Stubborn Disbelievers will never believe, no matter what Signs and Wonders they see.*

**وَلَوْ فَتَحْنَا عَلَيْهِم بَابًا مِّنَ السَّمَاءِ فَظَلُّوا فِيهِ يَعْرُجُونَ** — "And even if We opened to them a gate to the heavens and they were to continue ascending through it."

Allah is explaining the **extent** of their disbelief and their stubborn resistance to the truth, says Ibn Kathir, by stating that even if a door to heaven were to be opened for them, and they were to be taken up through it, they would *still* not believe.

Grasp how extreme the supposition is. It is not a small sign glimpsed at a distance. It is the sky itself opened, and these men climbing through it — continuing to ascend, as Ibn Kathir's rendering has it, *all day long*, and answering only *in the evening*. Every excuse about insufficient evidence is stripped away in advance. And still, in ayah 15, the answer comes back:

**لَقَالُوا إِنَّمَا سُكِّرَتْ أَبْصَارُنَا بَلْ نَحْنُ قَوْمٌ مَّسْحُورُونَ** — "They would surely say: 'Our eyes have been (as if) dazzled. Nay, we are a people bewitched.'"

### What "our eyes have been dazzled" means

The early authorities Ibn Kathir cites read **سُكِّرَتْ أَبْصَارُنَا** in slightly different ways, and together they give the full picture of a mind refusing what it has just seen:

- **Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and Ad-Dahhak**, as the commentary names them: *"our vision has been blocked."*
- **Qatadah, narrating that Ibn 'Abbas said**: *"our eyesight has been taken away."*
- **Al-'Awfi, reporting that Ibn 'Abbas said**: *"we were confused and put under a spell."*
- **Ibn Zayd**: *"The one who is dazzled [literally, intoxicated] is the one who cannot reason."*

Ibn Zayd's note is the key to the word. It carries the sense of being made drunk: a person so overwhelmed that he can no longer reason from what is in front of him. That is precisely the excuse being put in their mouths, and Ibn Kathir's rendering spells out what the claim amounts to — *we have not seen any angel or heaven*. Faced with heaven itself, they do not say "this is false". They say instead: *the instrument is broken. Our eyes are not working.*

And then they go one step further, which is the real point of ayah 15: **بَلْ نَحْنُ قَوْمٌ مَّسْحُورُونَ** — "Nay, we are a people bewitched." First they blame their eyes; then, in case that is not enough, they say something has been done to them — they have been put under a spell. Al-'Awfi's report from Ibn 'Abbas ties the two together: confused, and under a spell.

This is what makes the passage so quietly devastating. The disbelief described in ayat 12–13 is not an evidential position at all. It is a stance that will convert *any* evidence, including an open door to the sky, into a fresh reason not to believe.

## Living it

**Mockery is not a verdict.** Ayat 10–11 settle this once: being mocked was the ordinary experience of the Messengers themselves — Ibn Kathir says no Messenger came to a nation but they rejected him and mocked him. If ridicule were a measure of falsehood, every prophet would have failed the test. When a believer is mocked today for prayer, for modesty, for taking revelation seriously, the ayah does not tell him to feel nothing — it tells him he is in known company.

**Know the people you speak to.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's point about فِی rather than اِلٰی is a whole method of calling people to Allah — what is called *daʿwah*, inviting others to the truth — folded into one preposition: the messenger was sent *from among* the people so they would find it easy to trust him, and being one of them, he knew their taste and temperament and planned his work for their reform accordingly. Truth is not softened; it is delivered by someone who knows the room.

**Stop expecting one more argument to do the work.** Ayat 14–15 are a mercy for anyone exhausted by a family member or friend who answers every proof with a new objection. Allah Himself states that some would not believe even if a door to heaven were opened and they were taken up through it. Present the truth, and then leave the outcome with the One who owns hearts — the burden of forcing conviction was never yours.

**Guard the door of your own heart.** The sobering thing about ayah 12 is *whose* hearts are described — those, in Ibn Kathir's words, too stubborn and too arrogant to follow Allah's guidance. Arrogance towards the truth is not a harmless personality trait. The safest habit a believer can build is the readiness to be corrected, especially when the correction is unwelcome.

**And take the second half of the precedent as your own.** The example of the ancients that ayah 13 invokes ends, for the believers, in rescue — Allah saved His Prophets and their followers, Ibn Kathir says, in this world and in the Hereafter. That is the same well-known record. It just reads very differently depending on which side of it you are standing on.

passages.title: The adorned sky guarded from every devil
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** In these three ayat Allah lifts the reader's eyes upward. He placed the *burūj* in the sky, He adorned it, and He guarded it from every accursed devil — and even the one who tries to steal a hearing is pursued by a clear flame. The exception itself shows the guard at work. Ayat 16–18 are one connected movement: the heaven above you is not empty space, it is a *guarded* place.

## Where this comes in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the sequence. The verses just before this described the doggedness and hostility of the deniers and disbelievers. In this verse and those that follow immediately after, clear proofs of the Oneness, Knowledge and Power of Allah have been given, and described alongside them is what transpires before His creation between the heavens and the earth. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's comment is that a little deliberation on this, on the part of a sensible person, would make any denial impossible.

So the argument is not merely "look how beautiful the sky is." The same sky you gaze at is under guard — and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān will spell out further down, that guarding has a purpose bound up with revelation itself.

## Ayah 16: the *burūj* in the sky

**وَلَقَدْ جَعَلْنَا فِي السَّمَاءِ بُرُوجًا وَزَيَّنَّاهَا لِلنَّاظِرِينَ** — "Indeed, We have placed *burūj* in the sky, and adorned it." The translation in our text renders *burūj* as "constellations"; Ibn Kathir's rendering of the ayah is "We have put the big stars in the heaven and We beautified it for the beholders."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that **burūj** is the plural of **burj**, a word applied to big palaces and castles and to similar other structural entities. That is its everyday sense: a large, raised, built structure.

Two explanations of what the word points to here reach us from the early authorities, and our sources report them side by side rather than ruling between them:

- **The big stars / heavenly bodies.** Ibn Kathir reports this from **Mujahid** and **Qatadah**; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names **Mujahid, Qatadah, Abu Salih and others** for the same explanation. Ibn Kathir adds his own supporting comment, citing the parallel ayah *"Blessed be He Who has placed the burūj in the heavens"* (25:61).
- **Sentinel fortresses.** This is the wording of **ʿAtiyah al-ʿAwfi**, quoted by Ibn Kathir: "Buruj here refers to sentinel fortresses."

It is worth simply noticing the vocabulary Allah chose. The root sense of *burj* is a fortified structure, and the very next ayah tells us the sky is guarded.

Ibn Kathir's own summary of the ayah is worth sitting with: to those who ponder, and who look repeatedly at the dazzling signs and wonders to be seen in the creation, Allah mentions His creation of the heavens with their immense height, and both the fixed and the moving heavenly bodies with which He has adorned them.

**Which "sky"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on the word **as-samāʾ**. It notes that here as-samāʾ means the atmosphere — what modern terminology calls "space" — and that the application of the word in both senses is common and recognised: deep space is called as-samāʾ, and the atmosphere much lower than it is also repeatedly termed as-samāʾ in the Qur'an. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defers the fuller investigation of stars and planets, coordinated with classical and modern astronomy, to its comments on 25:61.) This is not a side note — it matters when Maʿārif ul Qurʼān returns, further down, to the question of *where exactly* the devils were sitting to eavesdrop.

**"And adorned it."** The verb *zayyannā* is first-person: Allah Himself did the adorning. The beauty of the night sky is deliberate. And in Ibn Kathir's rendering, *"for the beholders"* attaches that beauty to an audience — and his phrasing tells you who really qualifies as a beholder: the one who ponders and returns his gaze again and again to these signs.

## Ayah 17: "And We protected it from every accursed devil"

**وَحَفِظْنَاهَا مِن كُلِّ شَيْطَانٍ رَّجِيمٍ** — the third of three divine verbs in a row: *We placed*, *We adorned*, *We protected*. Adornment and protection sit together here. The sky is both a display and something under guard.

**Rajīm** is rendered "outcast" in Ibn Kathir's text and "accursed" in the translation of the ayah — the devil who has been driven away. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān will fill in exactly what that expulsion refers to in a moment. And note *kull*, "**every**" accursed devil: the guard is stated over the whole class, before ayah 18 gives its one qualification.

## Ayah 18: "except the one who steals a hearing"

**إِلَّا مَنِ اسْتَرَقَ السَّمْعَ فَأَتْبَعَهُ شِهَابٌ مُّبِينٌ.** Ibn Kathir's rendering is literally "except him who steals the hearing" — the word carries the sense of theft. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes these devils in exactly those terms: they would enter the atmospheric zone *like thieves*, sit there *in ambush*, and hear a little *by stealth*. This is not a devil who has been permitted to listen. He is a thief.

And he is pursued. **Shihāb mubīn** — a flaming fire that is *mubīn*, clear, visible. Ibn Kathir describes the scene: Allah made the shooting stars to guard the heaven against the evil devils who try to listen to information conveyed at the highest heights; if any devil breaches it and advances hoping to listen, a clear shooting star comes to him and destroys him. He may, however, already have passed on what he heard, before the fire hit him, to another devil below him — and that one takes it to his friends among the humans. Ibn Kathir notes that this is stated in the Sahih.

That last detail is the hinge. It explains how any true word ever reaches a fortune-teller at all.

## From the Sunnah: what they are trying to overhear

Explaining this ayah, **al-Bukhari** reported from **Abu Hurayrah** that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "When Allah decrees any matter in heaven, the angels beat their wings in submission to His Word, [with a sound like] a chain [beating] on a smooth rock."

Ibn Kathir's text notes here that ʿAli and other subnarrators said, "The sound reaches them." The narration continues: "When the fright leaves their (angels') hearts, they are asked: 'What did your Lord say?' They respond: 'The truth. And He is the Most High, the Most Great.' So those who hope to hear something listen, and they are standing one above the other."

**Sufyan**, one of the narrators, described them with a gesture — spreading the fingers of his right hand and holding it so that the fingers were above one another. The narration goes on: "Sometimes the flaming fire hits one of these listeners before he is able to convey what he has heard to the one who is beneath him, and he is burned up, or sometimes the fire does not hit him until he has [passed it] on to the one beneath him, so he brings it to the earth."

Ibn Kathir's text then introduces the closing portion with a transmitter's hedge — "Perhaps Sufyan said" — before giving these words:

> "…until it reaches the earth and he puts it into the mouth of the sorcerer or fortune-teller, so that after telling a hundred lies he gets something right, and the people say, 'Did he not tell us that on such and such a day such and such would happen, and we found it to be the truth among the statements which were heard from heaven.'"

Read that slowly and several things land at once.

**First, the awe of the angels.** These are creatures of obedience, and yet the decree of Allah reaches them with a fright that has to *leave* their hearts before they can speak. Their answer is not a report of information but a confession: *the truth — and He is the Most High, the Most Great.* Ahl al-Sunnah, the mainstream of the Muslim community, receive reports like this as they came, in the way of the Salaf — the earliest Muslim generations: affirming what is said of Allah without likening Him to His creation, without asking "how," and without emptying the words of their meaning.

**Second, the smallness of the enemy's enterprise.** The devils' whole undertaking, stacked in a ladder up through the dark, is to catch something of a decree that was never addressed to them — and by this description, the flame may reach a listener before he has even passed it down, and he is burned up.

**Third — and this is the practical payload — the arithmetic of the fortune-teller.** One stolen word, relayed down a chain of thieves, buried in *a hundred lies*, and the customer remembers the one thing that came true. The narration is not merely conceding that soothsayers sometimes hit the mark; it names what the hit actually is, and what surrounds it.

## When did the guarding begin?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān devotes its main discussion here to a genuinely puzzling question, and it is worth following the reasoning carefully.

**The first thing these verses prove, it says, is that the shayāṭīn have no access to the heavens.** But that accursed devil was in the heavens at the time of the creation of Sayyidna Adam (peace be upon him), and it was there that he deceived Adam and Hawwa (peace be upon them) — events which took place before they appeared on the earth. Up to that time, the entry of the jinn and the shayāṭīn into the heavens was not prohibited. It was **after** the coming down of Sayyidna Adam and the expulsion of the devil that this entry was banned.

Then what were they doing later, in the period before the Prophet ﷺ? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān turns to Surah al-Jinn: *"And we used to sit in ambush at places from it so as to eavesdrop. Whoever then tries to hear would find for him a flame in hot pursuit"* (72:9). From this, it says, it appears that before the coming of the Prophet ﷺ the shayāṭīn could overhear things happening in the heaven through the mutual conversation of the angels — and it is careful to add that this **does not necessarily imply** that they heard such information *by entering into* the heavens. The phrase it highlights, *naqʿudu minhā maqāʿid* — rendered above as "we used to sit in ambush at places from it" — gives the sense that they would enter the atmospheric zone where clouds abound, like thieves, sit there in ambush, and hear. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds that these words themselves indicate that the ban on the jinn and the shayāṭīn entering the heavens had continued in force; they would reach the outer atmosphere of the skies and hear a little by stealth.

**But how could they hear a conversation of angels taking place inside the heavens while they were outside it?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that this is not something impossible. It is quite probable that the heavenly bodies are not prohibitive of the transmission of sound, and it is also not far-fetched that the angels sometimes come lower down the heavens and engage in some conversation. It cites a hadith of **Sayyidah ʿAʾishah** appearing in the **Sahih of al-Bukhari** as confirming this very probability: she said that the angels sometimes come down as far as where the clouds are and talk about the heavenly happenings among themselves. It was in that atmospheric zone of the skies that the shayāṭīn used to hide in order to hear this news.

**Then came the advent of the Prophet ﷺ**, and an additional arrangement was activated: the shayāṭīn were stopped even from this covert eavesdropping, through meteors or shooting stars — *al-Shihāb al-Thāqib* — which zoom in upon them from the outer space with enormous speed.

And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the purpose plainly: according to the statements of the Qur'an, it appears that these *shihābs* or flames are formed to hit the shayāṭīn **in order that the revelation remains protected**. In other words, they are driven away by these flames so that they would not overhear the angels.

## "But shooting stars existed before Islam"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious objection honestly. The presence of shooting stars in outer space is nothing new; falling stars were seen even before the coming of the Prophet ﷺ, and the phenomenon continues after him as well. If so, how can it be said that shooting stars show up to drive the shayāṭīn away, as a particular feature of *his* age? Obviously, this seems to support the view of the scientists — that meteors become so hot from rushing through the air that they glow and often burn up, which gives onlookers the impression that a star has fallen. Arabic itself has the expression *inqiḍāḍ al-kawkab*, a virtual synonym for the falling of a star.

**The answer given is that there is no contradiction here.** One or more scientific explanations may well be possible — vapours rising from the earth's surface heating up at some point, or the speed of the meteors making them glow and burn, or a flame emitted from a star — and this may have habitually continued since ever. But **before** the coming of the Prophet ﷺ these flames were not employed to serve a particular purpose. After his coming, meteoric flames were employed to serve the purpose of shooting the shayāṭīn who would come up to stealthily hear the conversation of the angels.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān attributes this interpretation to **ʿAllamah al-Alusi** in *Ruh al-Maʿani*, where he reports that someone put it to the hadith authority **Imam Zuhri** that stars used to fall even before the coming of the Prophet ﷺ. He said: "Yes." The questioner then confronted him with the verse. He replied: "The shooting stars, no doubt, did exist before — but, after the coming of the Holy Prophet ﷺ, when the shaitans were dealt with sternly, these were employed to drive them away."

And in a hadith in the **Sahih of Muslim**, there is a narration from **Sayyidna Ibn ʿAbbas** reporting the Prophet's ﷺ own words on this subject. He was sitting with a group of his Companions when they saw a star falling. He asked them what they used to take the falling of a star to be during the days of Jāhiliyyah — that is, before Islam. They said: we took it to be a sign of some major upheaval in the world, or that a prominent man would die, or be born. He said: this is absurd; it has nothing to do with someone's death or birth. As for these flames, they are thrown to dispel the shayāṭīn.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up: the view of the scientists about shooting stars is not contrary to the Qur'an, and it is also not too far-fetched to state that these flames are made to fall directly from some stars. Whichever way it is taken, the purpose of the Qur'an stands proved clearly.

## Living it

**Become one of the *nāẓirīn*.** Ayah 16 says the sky was adorned, and Ibn Kathir's rendering names the audience: *for the beholders*. His beholder is the one who ponders and looks repeatedly at these dazzling signs. So actually go outside at night sometimes and look up, with the intention of remembering the One who placed the *burūj* there. The ayah presumes an audience; be part of it.

**Take confidence in the protection of revelation.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says it directly: these flames are formed to hit the shayāṭīn so that the revelation remains protected — they are driven off so that they would not overhear the angels. What reached the Prophet ﷺ is not of the same kind as what a thief snatches at the edge of the atmosphere.

**Kill the impulse to read the sky for your fate.** The Prophet ﷺ told his Companions plainly that a falling star has nothing to do with anyone's death or birth — that reading of the sky belonged to the days of Jāhiliyyah, before Islam. Whatever form that instinct takes in your own life, this passage empties it out.

**Remember the hundred lies.** When someone offers you the future — the sorcerer or fortune-teller of the narration, or any of his modern descendants — recall the chain that narration describes: a snatched word, a burning pursuer, a relay of thieves, and a hundred lies around the one thing that came out right.

**And measure the enemy correctly.** The devil of ayah 18 is *rajīm*: an outcast, driven away, banned from where he once had entry. He is not a rival power standing beside Allah. The sky is guarded, the flame is already stationed, and the guarding is Allah's own doing — *We placed*, *We adorned*, *We protected*.

passages.title: The earth spread out and its measured provision
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath.** Ayat 19–21 turn the reader's eye down to the ground underfoot and make a single sustained point: this earth was spread out, anchored and planted by Allah, and everything that grows on it or reaches you from it comes in an exact, deliberate amount that He alone sets.

What binds the three ayat into one unit is the idea of **measure**. In ayah 19 everything that grows does so *mawzūn* — rendered "in due proportion." In ayah 20 you are handed a living, and in the same breath told about others on your land whom you do not actually provide for. In ayah 21 the argument reaches its source: the supplies for every single thing are with Allah, and nothing is sent down except "in a known measure." The passage moves from the landscape, to your dinner table, to the treasury behind both.

## Where this sits: the turn from the heavens to the earth

Ibn Kathir gathers ayat 16–20 under one heading — "The Power of Allah and His Signs in the Heavens and on Earth" — and addresses it, in his words, "to those who ponder, and look repeatedly at the dazzling signs and wonders that are to be seen in the creation." Having spoken of the heavens, the passage pivots downward. In Ibn Kathir's summary:

> "Then Allah mentions His creation of the earth and how He spread it out, and the firm mountains, valleys, lands and sands that He has placed in it, and the plants and fruits that He causes to grow in their appropriate locations."

Notice what that pivot does to the argument. The earth is not a random surface you happen to have landed on; it is presented as part of the same display of power that the heavens above belong to. The One addressed in the heights is the One who set your mountains and grew your wheat.

## Ayah 19: three actions, one Doer

Ibn Kathir's rendering of the ayah is: "And We have spread out the earth, and have placed firm mountains in it, and caused all kinds of things to grow in it, in due proportion." Three actions follow one after another, and all three have the same subject:

- **We spread out the earth** — presented as something laid open, not a cramped ledge.
- **We placed firm mountains in it** — the things that hold fast.
- **We caused all kinds of things to grow in it** — and, Ibn Kathir adds, not only mountains but valleys, lands and sands, with the plants and fruits set "in their appropriate locations."

That last phrase is worth pausing on. The earth is not uniform, and that is the point: ridge and valley, sand and soil, and each growing thing placed where it belongs. Variation is not disorder here. It is arrangement.

No partner is named in any of the three actions. The ayah attributes the spreading, the anchoring and the growing to Allah alone.

## The heart of the passage: *min kulli shay'in mawzūn*

Ayah 19 ends with a phrase the commentators dwell on: **مِن كُلِّ شَيْءٍ مَّوْزُونٍ** — rendered by Ibn Kathir as "all kinds of things in due proportion," and by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as "everything in balance." Both renderings point at the same thing: an amount that has been determined rather than left loose.

**The first reading: predetermined amounts.** Ibn 'Abbas said this means that the things which grow do so with their predetermined proportions. Ibn Kathir then names others who held the same view: Sa'id bin Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, Abu Malik, Mujahid, Al-Hakim bin 'Utaybah, Al-Hasan bin Muhammad, Abu Salih and Qatadah.

**Why measure is a mercy.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes this reading and presses on it with an argument that repays slow reading. It was Allah's wisdom, it says, that made everything grow in a determined measure — *not less* than what would have made life difficult, and *not too much*, because excess would have brought difficulties of a different nature. Then it runs the experiment: suppose grains like wheat and rice, and the best of fruits, grew in such excess that stockpiles remained even after people and animals had consumed them liberally. Those stores would go bad. Keeping them in ideal natural condition through varying conditions would be difficult. And if they had to be dumped, not much space would be left for such mega dumpings.

Its conclusion is striking: it was within Allah's power to make grains and fruits grow so abundantly that everyone would have them free everywhere, with stores upon stores left lying around despite care-free use — but *that situation could have turned into a punishment for human beings*. So provision was given in a particular measure and balance for two reasons, both stated plainly: **so that its worth and value remains actively recognised**, and **so that it is not left over only to go to waste**.

This reframes something most of us experience as a defect. The fact that food must be sought, grown, paid for and used carefully is not a gap in the design. It is the design — and it is what keeps a loaf of bread meaningful.

**The second reading: proportion as beauty.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers a second sense of *mawzūn*, and presents it as also legitimate rather than ruling it out. Allah has created everything that grows in a suitable and proportionate manner which gives it beauty and attraction. Trees are different; so are their trunks, branches, leaves, flowers and fruits — different in size, shape, colour and taste. What anyone readily sees is their happy balance and delightful looks; everyone enjoys having them around. And then a line of real humility: a full comprehension of the wisdom which has gone into their making is not possible for any human being.

So the phrase is read as covering both the quantity and the form: the right amount, and the right shape. The same measure that keeps a harvest from going bad also makes a tree pleasant to stand under.

## Ayah 20: a living for you — and mouths you do not fill

**وَجَعَلْنَا لَكُمْ فِيهَا مَعَايِشَ** — "And We have provided therein means of living, for you." Ibn Kathir's gloss keeps the emphasis on multiplicity: Allah created the earth with **different means of provisions and livelihood of all kinds**.

Then the ayah adds a phrase that quietly dismantles a very natural piece of self-importance: **وَمَن لَّسْتُمْ لَهُ بِرَازِقِينَ** — "and for those whom you provide not."

- **Mujahid** said this refers to the riding animals and the cattle.
- **Ibn Jarir** widened it: "They are slaves, men and women, as well as the animals and the cattle." His summary of the point is worth quoting closely — Allah is reminding them of the ways of earning provision that He has made easy for them, and of the animals that He has subjugated for them to ride and to eat, and the slaves from whom they benefit, "but the provision of all of these comes from Allah alone."

Read that against daily life. You fill the trough, you pay the wage, you put the meal on the table for your household. It is entirely natural to feel that you are their provider. The ayah lets you keep the labour and takes back the title: *you are not their providers*. What you are doing is passing along, with your hands, something whose provision comes from Allah alone.

That is also, if you let it be, a relief. The weight of feeding those who depend on you was never actually resting on your shoulders alone.

## Ayah 21: the supplies, and the known measure

With this ayah Ibn Kathir opens a new heading: **"The Supplies for All Things are with Allah."**

**وَإِن مِّن شَيْءٍ إِلَّا عِندَنَا خَزَائِنُهُ** — "And there is not a thing, but the supplies for it are with Us."

Ibn Kathir's gloss is compact and total: Allah tells us that He is the Owner of all things, that everything is easy for Him, and that He has the supplies for all things with Him. The wording of the ayah is framed as a double negative — *there is not a thing except* that its supplies are with Us — and so it leaves nothing outside. Ibn Kathir keeps the explanation exactly where the ayah puts it: **ownership**, and **ease**.

**وَمَا نُنَزِّلُهُ إِلَّا بِقَدَرٍ مَّعْلُومٍ** — "and We do not send it down but in a known measure." Ibn Kathir explains: meaning, as He wills and as He wants, doing so out of His great wisdom and mercy towards His servants, **in a way that He is under no obligation to do — but He has decreed mercy for Himself.**

Hold the two halves of that together, because they protect each other. Nothing obliges Allah to send anything down; provision is not a debt owed to creation. And yet it comes, measured, because He has decreed mercy for Himself. That is a very different foundation for gratitude than entitlement.

Two things are being said about every gift that reaches you. First, the measure is **known** — known to Him, even when it looks to you like accident or shortage. Second, it is **sent down**: an act, a decision, not an automatic overflow.

**The rain, as an illustration.** Ibn Kathir cites a report — Yazid bin Abi Ziyad, from Abu Juhayfah — that 'Abdullah said: "No year has more rain than another, but Allah divides the rain between them as He wills, it rains here a year and there a year." Then he recited this very ayah. Ibn Kathir notes that this was reported by Ibn Jarir.

That is an extraordinarily useful way to look at the world. On this report, the yearly total is not what fluctuates; the **division** of it is. What one place does not receive this year is not evidence that the supply has failed — it has been apportioned as Allah wills, here one year and there another.

## Living it

The passage does not end in a command, but it presses in a direction. A few things follow directly from what the sources say:

**Read your measure correctly.** If what grows comes in predetermined proportions, and the sending down is "in a known measure," then a tight month is not an oversight. It is a known measure, released by One who has decreed mercy upon Himself while being under no obligation at all.

**Stop envying an unmeasured life.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's point stands on its own: limitless supply could have turned into a punishment — the stores would go bad, keeping them would be difficult, and worth would stop being actively recognised. The friction in getting and keeping is part of how value stays visible.

**Handle your dependants as a channel, not a source.** Ayah 20 lets you keep the work — the wages, the fodder, the meals — and removes the title. Ibn Jarir's line is the whole lesson: "the provision of all of these comes from Allah alone." Do the work well; drop the self-congratulation, and the panic.

**Let the landscape argue.** Ibn Kathir frames all of this as signs for those who ponder and look repeatedly. The firm mountain, the valley, the tree with its particular leaf and colour and taste — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says plainly that no human being can fully comprehend the wisdom which has gone into their making. Looking well and admitting that is itself the response the passage is asking for.

passages.title: From the sending of rain to the gathering of all generations
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** In these four ayat the Qur'an moves from the wind that fertilizes the clouds, to the fresh water you drink, to the giving of life and death, to the day your Lord gathers everyone together. Ibn Kathir does not treat them as four separate topics: he comments on ayat 21–25 as a single block.

**What holds it together.** Ibn Kathir opens the block by saying that Allah is telling us **He is the Owner of all things**, that everything is easy for Him, and that He has the supplies for all things with Him. That claim then unfolds: the rain is His to send and yours only to receive (ayah 22); the giving of life and the causing of death are His, and He is the Inheritor (ayah 23); His knowledge covers the first and the last of them (ayah 24); and He will gather them (ayah 25). Ibn Kathir names the thread himself when he reaches ayah 23 — this is about **His power to initiate creation and to renew it**.

## Backdrop: "in a known measure" (ayah 21)

*This section is context, not the passage itself.* Because Ibn Kathir's commentary on our ayat begins at ayah 21, a word about it helps.

On *"and We do not send it down but in a known measure"* he writes: **meaning, as He wills and as He wants** — doing so out of His great wisdom and mercy towards His servants, **in a way that He is under no obligation to do. But He has decreed mercy for Himself.**

That last sentence is worth pausing on. In Ibn Kathir's framing, the rain is not a debt Allah owes you; it is mercy He has decreed upon Himself.

He then cites a narration — Yazid bin Abi Ziyad reported from Abu Juhayfah that 'Abdullah said: *"No year has more rain than another, but Allah divides the rain between them as He wills, it rains here a year and there a year"* — and then he recited *"And there is not a thing, but the supplies for it are with Us."* Ibn Kathir notes this was **reported by Ibn Jarir**. What varies, on this narration, is the dividing, not the supply.

## "We send the winds fertilizing" (ayah 22)

Ayah 22 opens with **وَأَرْسَلْنَا الرِّيَاحَ لَوَاقِحَ**. Ibn Kathir explains it in two directions at once: the winds fertilize **the clouds**, so that they give rain, and they fertilize **the trees**, so that they open their leaves and blossoms. Sky and soil, in one phrase.

**Why the plural.** Ibn Kathir draws attention to something easy to walk past. Here the winds are mentioned in the **plural** form, he says, **because they give results** — unlike the barren wind (*Ar-Rih Al-'Aqim*, see Adh-Dhariyat 51:41), which is mentioned in the **singular** and described as barren, since it does not produce anything. His stated reason: **results can only be produced when there are two or more things.** The number of the noun is carrying part of the meaning.

**How the early scholars pictured it.** 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud said, *"The wind is sent bearing water from the sky, then it fertilizes the clouds until rain begins to generously fall, just as the milk of the pregnant camel flows generously."* Ibn Kathir adds that this was also the opinion of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibrahim An-Nakha'i and Qatadah. Ad-Dahhak said Allah sends it to the clouds, *"and it gets fertilized and becomes full of water."* 'Ubayd bin 'Umayr Al-Laythi described a sequence: Allah sends the wind which stirs up the earth, then the wind which raises clouds, then the wind which forms clouds, then the fertilizing wind which pollinates the trees — and then he recited this ayah.

Look at the images these scholars reached for in explaining the ayah: fertilizing, pregnancy, flowing milk. They are describing a system that is alive and giving, and telling you Who sends it.

## Sweet water out of a salt sea

*Maʿārif ul Qurʾān* dwells on the stretch of ayah 22 from *"And We send forth winds"* to *"and you are not able to store it."* It reads the phrasing as a hint to a **wise arrangement** — a formidable system established to provide water for all human beings, animals, cattle, birds and beasts living on this earth, as and when they need it: everywhere, under all conditions, for drinking or bathing or washing or irrigating farms and trees. And, it stresses, **this is water at no cost**. Those who spend on digging a well or laying pipes are paying only for the means and facilities. As it puts it: no one can pay for even a drop of water, nor has anyone been asked to pay for it.

It then traces the stages:

- **Lifting.** Vapours are created in the sea, generating the substance of rain, and the winds transform it into clouds — *Maʿārif* likens them to mountain-like planes laden with water.
- **Routing.** Those "giant planes" carry their cargo to every nook and corner of the world, raining down a specific quantity over a specific area, under Divine command — water home-delivered from the sea to all inhabitants of the earth, human and animal alike, including wildlife that is not within the range of human inquiry.
- **Desalination.** *Maʿārif* asks why the sea is salt at all, and answers with wisdom rather than complaint. The sea is home to countless life forms and their burial place too, and foul water from all over the earth ultimately drains into it. Had it been sweet water, it would have gone bad within a day, and its stench would have become a health hazard for those living on land. So it was made brackish enough to burn up the filth that keeps reaching it from all over the world. And yet — without the huge mechanised plants we build for the purpose — in the time between the vapours rising and the rain falling, the salt separates and what reaches you is sweet. It cites *"We gave you water to drink which quenches thirst"* (Al-Mursalāt 77:27), noting that **furāt** signifies thirst-quenching sweet water.

Ibn Kathir makes the same point on **فَأَسْقَيْنَاكُمُوهُ**: *"We send it down to you fresh and sweet, so that you can drink it; if We had wished, We could have made it salty (and undrinkable)."* He supports it from Sūrat Al-Wāqiʿah — *"Tell Me! The water that you drink, is it you who cause it to come down from the rain clouds, or are We the cause of it coming down? If We willed, We verily could make it salty, why then do you not give thanks?"* (56:68–70) — and from *"He it is Who sends water down from the sky; from it you drink and from it grows the vegetation on which you send your cattle to pasture"* (16:10). *Maʿārif* cites the same passage of Al-Wāqiʿah.

## "And it is not you who are the owners of its supply"

The ayah closes with **وَمَا أَنتُمْ لَهُ بِخَازِنِينَ**, which *Maʿārif* renders "and you are not able to store it."

Ibn Kathir's gloss: *"You are not taking care of it; rather We send it down and take care of it for you, making springs and wells flourish on the earth."* If Allah so willed, He could make it disappear — but by His mercy He sends it down and makes it fresh and sweet, maintaining the springs, wells and rivers, so that people may drink from it all year long, water their livestock and irrigate their crops.

*Maʿārif* turns this into a thought experiment. Living things need water every day, rather every moment. Rain every day of the year would have met the need — and, it observes, would have affected health and caused gridlock in transportation, hazards in movement and sluggishness in business. Rain concentrated in a few months, with each person holding a personal quota in personal custody, would have required every human being to assemble containers for three to six months of water — and the water would have gone bad within a few days. So the storage was built into the world instead: some of the rain is put to use immediately, helping farms and trees to bloom and people and animals to quench their thirst; part of it is deposited and preserved in open ponds and lakes; a greater portion is turned into ice — *Maʿārif* calls it a frozen sea — set atop mountain peaks where neither dust nor filth can touch it, seeping into the pores of the mountains and becoming the streams; and where there are no streams, water keeps flowing under the earth's surface **like human veins**, in every region of the world. Dig a well, it comes out.

*Maʿārif* then counts the blessings folded into that one short phrase: **the creation of water itself; making it reach all regions of the earth; making it potable; giving human beings the opportunity to drink it; the formidable system of collecting and preserving it according to need; and the ability to actually benefit from it** — since water may be available while circumstances or calamities, natural or man-made, leave a person unable to drink it. It reads the phrase as a hint to all of these, and also as a warning to those who refuse to see the truth as it is, closing with the Qur'an's words: *"Blessed is Allah, the best of creators."*

## "It is We Who give life, and cause death, and We are the Inheritors" (ayah 23)

Ibn Kathir: here Allah tells us of **His power to initiate creation and renew it**. He is the One Who brings life to creatures out of nothingness, then He causes them to die, then **He will resurrect all of them on the Day when He will gather them together**.

**"And We are the Inheritors."** Ibn Kathir's explanation is brief and total: **He will inherit the earth and everyone on it, and then it is to Him that they will return.**

## "And indeed, We know the first generations of you" (ayah 24)

Ibn Kathir presents ayah 24 as the next step in the same argument: after telling us that He will resurrect them all on the Day He gathers them, *"Then He tells us about His perfect knowledge of them, the first and the last of them."*

**Ibn 'Abbas** said: *"The first generations are all those who have passed away since the time of Adam. The present generations and those who will come afterward refer to those who are alive now and who are yet to come, until the Day of Resurrection."* Ibn Kathir adds that something similar was narrated from 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, Ad-Dahhak, Qatadah, Muhammad bin Ka'b, Ash-Sha'bi and others.

*Maʿārif ul Qurʾān* gathers **five** interpretations of *al-mustaqdimīn* ("those who go ahead") and *al-mustaʾkhirīn* ("those who remain behind"), reported from authorities among the Companions and the generation after them:

1. Those born to date, and those not yet born — **Qatadah and 'Ikrimah**.
2. The dead, and those alive till now — **Ibn 'Abbas and Ad-Dahhak**.
3. Good people who came before the appearance of the Ummah of the Prophet ﷺ, and his Ummah itself — **Mujahid**.
4. People who obey Allah and do good deeds, and people who disobey Him and neglect what is good — **Hasan and Qatadah**.
5. People who remain ahead in the rows of prayer, in the front lines of jihad, and in other righteous deeds — and those who remain behind in these deeds of merit, stay in the rear rows and are used to being late — **Hasan al-Basri, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Qurtubi, al-Sha'bi and others**.

*Maʿārif* judges that there is no real conflict or contradiction between these sayings: they can be accommodated all in one, because the all-encompassing knowledge of Allah covers all kinds of people who "go ahead" or "remain behind."

**A recorded disagreement.** Ibn Kathir preserves an exchange on exactly this point. **Ibn Jarir reported from Muhammad bin Abi Ma'shar, from his father, that he heard 'Awn bin 'Abdullah discussing this ayah with Muhammad bin Ka'b**, and it was stated that it refers to the rows for prayer. **Muhammad bin Ka'b said, "This is not the case"** — holding that *al-mustaqdimīn* refers to those who are dead or have been killed, and *al-mustaʾkhirīn* to those who have yet to be created — and he recited ayah 25 to finish the point. **'Awn bin 'Abdullah said, "May Allah help you and reward you with good."** (Muhammad bin Ka'b is also among those Ibn Kathir lists as narrating something similar to Ibn 'Abbas's reading.)

So the sources before us record both positions: one authority explicitly declining the prayer-row reading as the meaning of the ayah, while al-Qurtubi, Hasan al-Basri, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Sha'bi and others adopt it. Both are reported, and neither should be presented as the only reading.

**What al-Qurtubi draws from it.** In his Tafsir, al-Qurtubi says this verse indicates the merit of performing the prayer in the first row, and soon after its time becomes due. He notes this accords with the hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said that if people were to find out the enormous merit of calling the adhan and standing in the first row, everyone would have made the effort to stand there, and when no space remained for everybody, lots would have to be drawn. (*Maʿārif* cites this hadith without naming a collection, so it is left as reported there.)

Alongside it, al-Qurtubi reports a saying of **Sayyidunā Ka'b**: *"There are some people in this Ummah who, when they put their forehead on the ground for their sajdah, forgiveness is granted to all those who are praying behind them."* For that reason Ka'b liked to be in the **last** row, hoping that perhaps in the front rows there might be some servant of Allah of that class, through whose barakah — blessed presence — he too might be forgiven.

*Maʿārif* balances the two: what is apparent is that the real merit does lie in praying in the first row, as stands proved from the clear statements of the Qur'an and Sunnah; but a person who for some reason finds no place there has a merit of his own, in that some righteous servant of Allah may be praying in the front rows for whose sake he too may be forgiven. And it adds that just as the merit of the first row of prayer is drawn from this verse, so is the superiority of being in the front lines of jihad.

## "And verily your Lord will gather them together" (ayah 25)

The passage lands where Ibn Kathir said it was heading: **وَإِنَّ رَبَّكَ هُوَ يَحْشُرُهُمْ ۚ إِنَّهُ حَكِيمٌ عَلِيمٌ** — *"And verily your Lord will gather them together. Truly, He is Most Wise, (and) Knowing."* This is the Day Ibn Kathir already named under ayah 23: the Day when He will resurrect all of them and gather them together. It is also the ayah Muhammad bin Ka'b recited to settle his reading of ayah 24.

The commentaries before us do not add a separate gloss on the two names that close the ayah, and it would be wrong to invent one. It is worth noticing, though, that both words have already surfaced in Ibn Kathir's own commentary on this same block: he spoke of Allah sending down the rain in a known measure **out of His great wisdom and mercy**, and of **His perfect knowledge of them, the first and the last of them**. We affirm these names as they are given — Most Wise and Knowing, in a manner befitting Him, without likening Him to His creation and without emptying the words of their meaning.

## Living it

*What follows is reflection on the material above, not further quotation from it.*
