They found out about his guests, and they came *pleased*. This is what a sin looks like when a whole society has absorbed it: no furtiveness left, no residue of shame, only appetite and good spirits. It is the single most chilling word in the passage, and it sets up the verdict Allah will deliver in ayah 72.

## Lot's plea (ayat 68–69)

*"Verily, these are my guests, so do not shame me. And have Taqwa of Allah, and do not disgrace me."*

Notice what Lot does **not** lead with. He does not open with the enormity of the act itself. He leads with a claim they might still feel: *ḍayfī*, "**my guests**." His whole appeal turns on that possessive — what is done to them is done to him. He sets two verbs of humiliation around a single command. The first, *fa-lā tafḍaḥūni*, is rendered in our sources as "do not shame me" and "do not embarrass me." The second, *wa lā tukhzūni*, as "do not disgrace me" and "do not humiliate me." Both are about *him*: not his safety, his face.

And placed exactly between them is the only argument that ever really mattered: **"and have taqwā of Allah"** — which the translation here renders "fear Allah." Taqwā is the mindfulness of Allah that makes a person guard himself against His displeasure: the awareness that Allah sees. Lot's plea is a small architecture: an appeal to human decency on one side, an appeal to human decency on the other, and taqwā as the load-bearing pillar in the middle. He is a prophet appealing on every register he has left.

## Their answer (ayah 70)

*"Did we not forbid you from entertaining (or protecting) any of the ʿālamīn?"*

Ibn Kathir glosses their meaning plainly: *"did we not tell you that you should not have anyone as a guest?"* — which is why the translation renders it "have we not forbidden you from protecting anyone."

Take in what that reveals. These men are not answering a moral appeal with a moral counter-argument. They answer by reminding him of **a prohibition they had already laid on him**: you were told not to take anyone in. Lot invokes taqwā of Allah; they invoke their own earlier ban on hospitality. Two moral universes talking past each other.

## "These are my daughters" (ayah 71)

*"These are my daughters, if you must act (so)."*

Ibn Kathir explains Lot's intent in one line: **"He reminded them about their womenfolk and what their Lord had created for them in the women of permissible sexual relationships."** In other words, he was pointing them back to the lawful channel Allah had created for that desire — which is why the translation supplies the bracketed *"so marry them"*. Read with Ibn Kathir's gloss, this is not a surrender of his daughters to the men of the city; it is a reminder of the door Allah opened, set against the one they were battering at. Ibn Kathir adds only that the matter "has already been explained and is no need to repeat the discussion here."

The conditional is worth hearing too — *"if you must act"*, *in kuntum fāʿilīn*. It is the voice of a man who has run out of arguments and is now bargaining.

## What they did not know (ayah 72)

Before the verdict, Ibn Kathir sets the clock for us: **"All of this happened while they were still unaware of the inevitable calamity and punishment that was about to befall them the following morning."**

That is the frame for everything above. The rejoicing, the prohibition thrown back in Lot's face, the whole confrontation — all of it is unfolding while a calamity is already fixed for the morning. They have never been closer to ruin and never felt further from it.

Hence the verdict: **"Verily, by your life, in their wild intoxication, they were wandering blindly."**

**Their "intoxication."** The word is *sakratihim*, rendered "wild intoxication" by Ibn Kathir and "intoxicated" in the translation. Our commentators do not read it as wine: Qatādah explained *"in their wild intoxication"* as meaning **"in their misguided state."**

**"Wandering blindly."** *Yaʿmahūn.* Qatādah said it means **"they were playing."** ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that it means **"they were confused."** Put those together and you have the picture: men misguided, larking, confused, wandering blindly — and enjoying themselves, on the far side of a morning that had already been decided.

This is the passage's most transferable warning. Sin can leave a person feeling perfectly clear-headed, sociable, even cheerful — while the sources describe exactly that state as intoxication and blind wandering.

## The oath — a great honour for the Prophet ﷺ

Now the astonishing turn. Mid-narrative, Allah stops addressing the story and addresses **you**: *laʿamruka* — "by your life."

The majority of the commentators, as reported in *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*, hold that the one addressed in *laʿamruka* is the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ; it is his life that Allah has sworn by. Ibn Kathir states it directly: "Allah swore by the life of His Prophet ﷺ, which is an immense honour reflecting his high rank and noble status."

On its meaning, Ibn Kathir gives: **"by your life and the length of your stay in this world"**, and ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās simply, *"by your life."* Maʿārif ul Qurʾān adds that it is an oath by "the age and life" of the Prophet ﷺ.

Why does that matter so much? Because of what an oath implies about the thing sworn by. Two reports in our sources converge on the same point:

- ʿAmr bin Mālik An-Nakarī reported from Abū Al-Jawzāʾ that **Ibn ʿAbbās** said: *"Allah has never created or made or formed any soul that is dearer to Him than Muhammad ﷺ. I never heard that Allah swore by the life of anyone else."* Ibn Kathir notes this was reported by Ibn Jarīr.
- Al-Bayhaqī in *Dalāʾil an-Nubuwwah*, and Abū Nuʿaym, Ibn Marduwayh and others, reported from **Ibn ʿAbbās** that Allah has not bestowed on anyone in the whole creation an honour and rank higher than that of Muhammad al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ — and that this is the reason Allah has never sworn by the life of any prophet or angel, while in this ayah He swears by the age and life of His Messenger ﷺ. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān calls it "the highest conceivable honour and deference accorded to him."

There is a quiet beauty in the placement. In the middle of describing the ugliest scene in the surah, Allah lifts His Messenger ﷺ to the highest station He has given any creature. The blindness of the townsmen and the honour of the Prophet ﷺ sit in the same sentence.

## Does this allow us to swear by other than Allah?

No — and Maʿārif ul Qurʾān treats the question carefully, because a reader could easily draw the wrong conclusion.

**The rule for us.** To swear by anyone or anything other than the names and attributes of Allah is not permissible for any human being. The reasoning is precise: one would only swear by whoever is held in the highest esteem — and, as is obvious, Allah alone can be the highest.

**From the Sunnah** (both reports exactly as our source cites them):

- The Prophet ﷺ said: *"Do not swear by your mothers, fathers and idols. And do not swear by anyone except Allah — and if you have to swear by Allah, do it only when you are truthful in your statement."* Reported by **Abū Dāwūd** and **An-Nasāʾī** from Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him).
- It appears in the *Ṣaḥīḥayn* — **the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Bukhārī and the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim** — that the Prophet ﷺ once saw ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him) swearing by his father. He called out to him and said: *"Watch out! Allah forbids swearing by fathers. Whoever has to take an oath, let him do it in the name of Allah; otherwise, let him be silent."*

**Why Allah's own oaths are different.** This injunction, Maʿārif explains, applies to Allah's creation in general. Allah Himself swears by different things He has created, and this is particular to Him; its purpose is to state the sublimity and beneficence of something from the desired angle. The cause of forbidding it to common people is simply not present in His case: in the Word of Allah there is no probability that He would take someone from His creation to be the highest and the best — because absolute greatness is particular only to Allah. So when Allah swears by the life of His Prophet ﷺ, He is not elevating a creature above Himself; He is telling creation what that life is worth to Him.

## Carrying it

**Guard the guest.** A prophet of Allah put his own honour on the line rather than let his guests be harmed, and his first word to the crowd was simply *"these are my guests."* That is the weight the scene places on whoever is under your protection.

**Lead with taqwā.** When Lot had nothing left, the argument he reached for was *"have taqwā of Allah."* It did not move them — but it was still the right thing to say, and a prophet is not judged by whether the crowd listens.

**Check your own sobriety.** The men of that city felt fine. They were rejoicing, confident, quoting their own prohibition back at a prophet — and the Qur'an describes them, in that very state, as wandering blindly in intoxication, with the morning already fixed. The passage asks a quiet question of anyone reading it: what am I currently *sure* about, while wandering?

**Love him ﷺ as Allah honoured him.** Allah swore by his life — and Ibn ʿAbbās said he never heard that Allah swore by the life of anyone else. That single word *laʿamruka* is worth pausing over every time it is recited.

passages.title: The blast at sunrise and the overturned cities
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat close the account of the people of Lut (peace be upon him): the punishment falls, and then the Qur'an stops the story and turns to us. What holds the passage together is the movement from **event** to **evidence** — ayat 73 and 74 tell what happened, and ayat 75 to 77 tell us that what happened is still lying there on a road people travel, waiting to be read by anyone with eyes to read it.

## The blast at sunrise (ayah 73)

Ayah 73 opens with the connective "So" — the punishment comes as the consequence of what the account of Lut's people has just described. What arrived was **al-Sayhah**. Ibn Kathir defines it plainly: "This is the piercing sound that came to them when the sun rose." Not a storm, not an army — a sound. A whole people were undone by a single noise.

The word closing the ayah is **مُشْرِقِينَ (mushriqin)**, which the translation renders "at sunrise," and Ibn Kathir's own phrasing keeps that hour in view: "when the sun rose." It is worth pausing on. The blast did not come in the dark, when a city is already braced for danger. It came at the hour a town wakes up and begins an ordinary day.

Ibn Kathir also reads the elements of the punishment as arriving together rather than as separate episodes. Commenting on "So the Sayhah overtook them," he says it was the piercing sound at sunrise, "which was accompanied by the city being flipped upside down, and stones of baked clay (As-Sijjil) raining down upon them." Sound, upheaval, and stones fell as one stroke — which is why the passage can move on so quickly to what the ruins now mean.

## "We made its top its bottom" (ayah 74)

The Arabic of ayah 74 is worth hearing literally. **فَجَعَلْنَا عَالِيَهَا سَافِلَهَا** — "We made *its high* (ʿāliyahā) *its low* (sāfilahā)." English translations say "turned upside down," which is accurate, but the Arabic sets two opposites side by side in bare, almost architectural terms: what was up, He made down. There is no verb of shaking or collapsing here; there is only Allah making the top into the bottom.

Then **حِجَارَةً (hijaratan)** — stones, which Ibn Kathir identifies as stones of baked clay, *al-sijjīl*. He does not expand on *sijjīl* in this place; he tells the reader that "the discussion of As-Sijjil in Surah Hud is a sufficient explanation." It is better to stop where he stopped than to fill the gap with speculation.

One phrase of Ibn Kathir's is worth noticing. Later in his comment he describes Sodom as the city "which was physically and spiritually turned upside down." He does not confine the overturning to the ground; his wording sets the physical and the spiritual beside each other in a single description of what that city became.

## "Signs for those who read signs" (ayah 75)

With ayah 75 the register changes completely. The story stops; the address begins.

The word the ayah uses for its audience is **الْمُتَوَسِّمِينَ (al-mutawassimin)**, and the translations in front of us circle around it rather than settling it: "those who see," "those who contemplate," and, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, "those who read signs." That last rendering catches something the others miss — the ayah says there are *āyāt* (signs) here for the *mutawassimīn*, and the point is that a sign only works when somebody is capable of reading it.

The early commentators quoted by Ibn Kathir give three complementary answers to who those people are:

- **Mujahid**: "those who have insight and discernment."
- **Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak**: those who *look*.
- **Qatadah**: "those who learn lessons."

Ibn Kathir then draws the strands together: the traces of that ruined city "are easily visible to any one who ponder about it, whether they look at it with physical eyesight or mental and spiritual insight." So there are two kinds of seeing in play, and the ayah is not choosing between them — the physical eye that actually goes and looks, and the inward eye that draws the conclusion. A person can have the first without the second and come away with nothing but a photograph.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds what is on display in these ruins: "great signs of the perfect power of Allah Taʿālā for those who believe and have the necessary hindsight and foresight." The commentary leaves those two words to speak for themselves; what it establishes is that the sign is available, and that a certain kind of person is needed to receive it.

## The ruins are on your route (ayah 76)

Ayah 76 is the hinge that makes the lesson unavoidable: **وَإِنَّهَا لَبِسَبِيلٍ مُّقِيمٍ** — the site lies on a road that *stays*. Ibn Kathir explains that the city of Sodom, "pelted with stones until it became a foul smelling lake (the Dead Sea), is on a route that is easily accessible until the present day." He connects it to Allah's words elsewhere: "Verily, you pass by them in the morning, and at night. Will you not then reflect?" (37:137-138).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the geography precisely. These ruined cities "fall on the main road which takes people from Arabia to Syria." This is not a legend set in some unreachable place; it is a location on a route that people actually travelled.

Maʿārif also brings in another ayah to sharpen the picture: of such settlements Allah says **لَمْ تُسْكَن مِّن بَعْدِهِمْ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا** — "not lived in after them except a little" (28:58); after the destruction, these habitations were not repopulated except for some. Putting the two indicators together, Maʿārif concludes that Allah made these ruined homes "a site from which coming generations could learn their essential lesson." The ruin was left standing as a lesson kept in place.

And it is still there. Maʿārif describes the site as lying in the proximity of Jordan, a wilderness below sea level, with a particular kind of water flowing across a major portion of it in which sea life cannot survive — "therefore, it is called the Dead Sea or the Sea of Lut (peace be upon him)."

## How the Prophet ﷺ passed such places

This is where the passage stops being history and becomes conduct.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that whenever the Prophet ﷺ passed by these sites, he went through a particular state in which he would be overwhelmed by the awe of Allah, his blessed head would lower, and he would try to make his mount hasten through. (The source describes this practice without naming a hadith collection, so it is given here only as Maʿārif reports it.)

Read that slowly. The one with the strongest faith and the clearest knowledge of Allah was the one most visibly moved at a place where Allah's punishment had landed. He did not linger, and he did not sightsee.

From this, Maʿārif draws a firm conclusion: this conduct of the Prophet ﷺ established the sunnah that making sites struck by divine punishment "a place of picnic and amusement is hard-heartedness at its ugliest." The only way to learn from such a place, it says, is to think about and *feel* the very presence of Allah's most perfect power on that ground, which should cause one to tremble with the fear of His punishment.

## "A sign for the believers" (ayah 77)

The passage ends by narrowing.

Notice the form of the word. Ayah 75 has **آيَات** — signs, plural — for those who read signs. Ayah 77 has **آيَة** — a sign, singular — for the believers. The English renderings vary, but in the Arabic the closing ayah gathers the whole episode into one thing to be seen.

And that one thing, on Ibn Kathir's reading, is larger than the destruction alone. He explains ayah 77 as meaning: "All that We did to the people of Lut, from the destruction and the vengeance, to how We saved Lut and his family, these are clear signs to those who believe in Allah and His Messengers." The sign is not only the ruin; it is the rescue. The same decree that ended one people carried Lut and his family out to safety. A believer who looks at the Dead Sea and sees only wrath has seen half the ayah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes here, with evident sorrow, what has actually happened at that site: the local Department of Archaeology set up hotels and residential quarters there to attract tourists, and "people with an incorrigible infatuation with the material" who are equally dismissive of the concerns of the Hereafter have made the site a place of fun and frolic, going there to enjoy the sights of the ancient. It is precisely against such heedlessness becoming a habit, Maʿārif says, that the Qur'an serves its warning at the end of the passage.

That is why the final ayah says "for the believers" after ayah 75 had said "for those who read signs." In reality, Maʿārif explains, these sites and the events attached to them are full of moral lessons for everyone having insight — "but it is the good fortune of believers only who would benefit by learning what these sites teach, while others would go through these sites as tourists and leave empty-handed."

That is the passage's last word, and it is a searching one. The evidence is public. The road is open. Two people can stand on the same shore of the same sea on the same morning; one leaves changed, the other leaves with souvenirs. The difference is not in the sign. It is in the one looking.

**Living it.** The passage sets an attitude, and it is a specific one: a site where Allah's punishment fell is not a place for amusement. Maʿārif is blunt about that, and the conduct of the Prophet ﷺ at such places is its evidence. But the wider demand of the passage is the one Qatadah names — the *mutawassim* is not simply someone who looks, but "those who learn lessons." Ibn Kathir's two kinds of seeing sit at the heart of this: physical eyesight, and mental and spiritual insight. Looking is easy and cheap. The question the ayah puts to us is whether anything we have seen has ever changed us.</tafsir>

passages.title: The Forest-dwellers and the people of al-Hijr
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These seven ayat come at the end of sūrah al-Ḥijr and deal with two peoples: the dwellers of *al-Aykah* — the forest-folk, who were the people of Shuʿayb (peace be upon him) — and the dwellers of *al-Ḥijr*, who are the people of Thamūd, who rejected their Prophet Ṣāliḥ (peace be upon him).

One thread runs visibly through both halves: the sources locate these ruins on ground people travel. Ibn Kathir explains the end of ayah 79, *"They are both on an open route, plain to see"*, as **"a visible route"**; and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places *al-Ḥijr* in a valley **between the Hijaz and Syria**. These are not stories from an unreachable corner of the world.

## Al-Aykah: the people of the intertwined trees

**The word itself.** Ibn Kathir reports from **Ad-Dahhak, Qatadah and others** that *al-Aykah* refers to **intertwined trees**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same core sense: *Aykah* means a dense forest. So these people are named after their landscape — the forest-folk — while the second nation in this passage is named after a valley of stone, *al-Ḥijr*.

**Who exactly were they?** Here the commentators genuinely differ, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the views rather than settling on one:

- Some commentators say that there was a dense forest near **Madyan**, so *Aykah* is actually a title of the people of Madyan — the same nation under a different name.
- Others have said that the people of Aykah and the people of Madyan were **two different peoples**, and that it was after the destruction of one of them that Shuʿayb (peace be upon him) was sent to the other.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then reports that in **Tafsīr Rūḥ al-Maʿānī** a *marfūʿ* hadith — that is, a report traced back to the Prophet ﷺ — appears **with reference to Ibn ʿAsākir**: *"Madyan and the people of Aikah are two peoples. Allah Taʿālā sent Shuʿayb to them."* Note carefully how this reaches us: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits it from Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, referred to Ibn ʿAsākir. No grading is given, and none should be assumed. Ibn Kathir, for his part, states simply that **the dwellers of al-Aykah were the people of Shuʿayb**, without entering the dispute.

For the reader, the disagreement is honest and the practical upshot is small: either way, the mission is Shuʿayb's, and the crime and the punishment are as described.

## What they actually did wrong (ayah 78)

Ayah 78 calls them *ẓālimīn* — wrongdoers. Ibn Kathir names three strands of their evildoing:

1. **Associating partners with Allah** (*shirk*) — the root corruption, a failure at the level of who is worshipped.
2. **Banditry** — highway robbery, violence against travellers.
3. **Cheating in weights and measures** — fraud in the marketplace, shaving a little off what is owed.

That combination is worth pausing on. Ibn Kathir's list runs from worship, to the road, to the scales. Their wrongdoing was not confined to a shrine; on this description, a traveller was not safe among them and neither was a customer.

**The punishment.** Ibn Kathir records that Allah punished them with the *Ṣayḥah* (the awful cry or torment), the earthquake, and the torment of the **Day of Shadow**.

## "So We took requital from them" (ayah 79)

The verb in ayah 79 is *fa-antaqamnā minhum* — rendered in the translation as *"so We inflicted punishment upon them"*, and by Ibn Kathir as *"So, We took vengeance on them."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's way of stating the same principle at the close of this sūrah is that Allah **"is to exact the full return from them of what they have been doing"** — the language of an account settled in full.

**"They are both on an open route, plain to see."** The second half of ayah 79 is the hinge of the whole passage. *Wa innahumā la-bi-imāmin mubīn* — **Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Ad-Dahhak and others** explained the phrase as **"a visible route"**.

Ibn Kathir draws out the geography: the dwellers of al-Aykah **lived near the people of Lūt, but at a later time**, and the people of Lūt were known to them. That, he says, is why Allah describes the two as being on an open route — and it is why Shuʿayb, warning his people, could say to them:

> *"And the people of Lūt are not far off from you!"* (Hūd 11:89)

Think about what that does to the argument. Shuʿayb is not asking his people to accept a report about a remote and unknown nation. He is pointing at a people whom, Ibn Kathir tells us, they already knew about — and the warning was still refused. The Qur'an then preserves the same logic for later listeners: the sites are described as lying on a visible route.

## Al-Hijr: Thamūd in the stone valley (ayat 80–82)

**Where it is.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies *al-Ḥijr* as a **valley situated between the Hijaz and Syria**, inhabited by the people of Thamūd. Again: on travelled ground between two known regions.

**"They denied the messengers" — why the plural?** Ibn Kathir says the dwellers of al-Ḥijr were **the people of Thamūd, who rejected their Prophet, Ṣāliḥ**. Yet ayah 80 says they denied *al-mursalīn*, "the messengers", in the plural. Ibn Kathir gives the principle behind the wording:

> **Whoever denies even one Messenger, then he has disbelieved in all of the Messengers** — thus they are described as rejecting "the Messengers".

That is a point of belief, not a stylistic flourish, and it is worth carrying carefully: on Ibn Kathir's principle, rejecting the one messenger who came to you is a rejection of all of them.

**"We gave them Our signs, but they turned away" (ayah 81).** Ibn Kathir explains that Ṣāliḥ brought them signs to prove that what he was telling them was true — such as **the she-camel, which Allah created for them out of a solid rock in response to Ṣāliḥ's supplication**. She grazed on their lands, and **the people and the camel took water on alternate days that were well known**.

Sit with the strangeness of that. A living animal brought out of solid rock — and what the account records next is that they resented the drinking arrangement enough to kill her. As Allah says of them elsewhere, quoted by Ibn Kathir:

> *"And as for Thamūd, We showed them and made the path of truth clear, but they preferred blindness to guidance."* (Fuṣṣilat 41:17)

**Preferred** blindness. That is the word ayah 81 is unpacking with *muʿriḍīn*, "turning away". On this reading, their problem was never a shortage of evidence.

When they rebelled and killed the she-camel, Ibn Kathir records that Ṣāliḥ said to them:

> *"Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. This is a promise which will not be belied."* (Hūd 11:65)

**"They carved their homes in the mountains, feeling secure" (ayah 82).** Ibn Kathir's reading of this ayah is sharp and unexpected. *Āminīn* — secure — means, he says, that **they were without fear and they had no real need for those houses; it was merely a form of extravagance and work without a purpose**.

So this is not praise of their engineering. On Ibn Kathir's reading it is an indictment of it: nobody was threatening them, and the houses met no real need. Effort on that scale, spent on nothing that was actually required. And in ayah 83, what reached them was a sound.

## From the Sunnah: the Prophet ﷺ at al-Hijr

Ibn Kathir says that this extravagance **could be seen from their work in the houses in al-Ḥijr, through which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed on his way to Tabūk**. He then describes what the Prophet ﷺ did as he passed: **he covered his head and urged his camel to go faster**, saying to his Companions:

> *"Do not enter the dwellings of those who were punished unless you are weeping, and if you do not weep then make yourself weep out of fear that perhaps what struck them may also strike you."*

(This is how Ibn Kathir relates the incident in his commentary on these ayat; he does not name a collection for it here, and neither will we.)

Read the whole scene, not only the words. He was travelling with his Companions and passed the very site whose stonework Ibn Kathir has just described. He did not stop to look. He veiled his head, hurried his camel, and gave his Companions an instruction about how such a place is to be entered at all.

**Three things this teaches, concretely:**

- **A punished site is not a place to admire.** Where Allah's judgement fell, the response the Prophet ﷺ modelled was to cover up and move on quickly, not to linger over the workmanship.
- **If the heart does not feel it, force it to.** "If you do not weep then make yourself weep" is a striking instruction. It tells us that the outward act, done deliberately, can be a way of summoning an inward state we lack.
- **The reason given is self-directed:** *out of fear that perhaps what struck them may also strike you*. Not "so you may pity them". These accounts are handed to us as a mirror.

## The morning of the fourth day (ayah 83)

*Fa-akhadhat-humu al-ṣayḥatu muṣbiḥīn* — the *Ṣayḥah*, which Ibn Kathir glosses as **the torment, the awful cry**, overtook them in the early morning. Ibn Kathir specifies the timing exactly: **the morning of the fourth day** — that is, the morning after the three days Ṣāliḥ had announced in Hūd 11:65.

Notice the precision. They were given a countdown, told openly that it was *"a promise which will not be belied"*, and told to spend those three days in their homes. Then it came, on schedule, in the early morning.

## "And all they achieved was of no help to them" (ayah 84)

Ibn Kathir reads ayah 84 with the whole story in view. What they "used to earn" means **all of the benefits that they used to gain from their crops and fruits, and the water** — the very water **they did not want to share with the she-camel, which they killed so that it would not reduce their share of the water**.

That is a devastating close. The thing they killed for is named as the thing that could not save them. In Ibn Kathir's words, **all of that wealth would not protect them or help them when the command of their Lord came to pass**.

**Living it.** The question the ayat put to a reader is not whether we have carved houses out of a mountain. It is whether we are running the same calculation: building security out of things that, as ayah 84 says, are of no help when the command of the Lord comes — and shaving other people's rights to protect our own share. Ayah 78's list — false worship, preying on travellers, cheating the scales — is not an ancient list.

## Why these stories sit at the end of the sūrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān supplies the frame that makes the placement make sense. **Described at the beginning of the sūrah was the hostility of the disbelievers of Makkah against the Holy Prophet ﷺ**, which also carried brief words of comfort for him. Now, at the end of the sūrah, **more words of comfort appear** to mollify his concern about their grudge and hostility.

That is the pastoral work these accounts are doing. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the reasoning that follows: the Prophet ﷺ is asked not to grieve over their hostile opposition, because **there is a day when all scores will be settled** — the Day of Judgement — and it is bound to come. Then there is the fact that Allah did not create the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them except **with truth and wisdom**. The wise consideration behind this creation is that people should believe in the existence of the Maker of the universe, attest to His Oneness and supremacy, and obey His injunctions — and, once Allah's argument stands established, that the defaulter be punished. Since that punishment does not seem to come in full here in this mortal world, it has to be somewhere else, at a fixed time: the Day of Judgement. **And this Hour is sure to come. Everyone will be taken care of there.**

This being the wise arrangement of things, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, let him not grieve. The better course for him is **to overlook their wicked behaviour in a gracious manner** — neither paying attention to their behaviour nor complaining about it — because his Lord is **great as Creator and great as the Master Knower as well**: He knows his patience and fortitude, and He knows the evil machinations of his enemies too. Therefore, **He is to exact the full return from them of what they have been doing**.

That is the emotional logic of ayat 78–84. Al-Aykah and al-Ḥijr are not history lessons dropped in at the end. They are evidence — described by the Qur'an itself as lying on a route that is plain to see — that the account is settled in full.

passages.title: Creation has a purpose, so forgive graciously and covet nothing
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** In the closing lines of Sūrat al-Ḥijr, Allah turns to His Prophet ﷺ personally and answers the hostility he was facing: the universe was not made without purpose, the Hour is certainly coming — and therefore the man being insulted by the disbelievers of Makkah can afford to let the insults go.

What binds ayat 85–88 into one unit is a single line of reasoning. A creation made "with the truth" (85) guarantees a day of reckoning; a Lord who is *al-Khallāq al-ʿAlīm* (86) guarantees He can and will bring it about; a Prophet ﷺ who has already been given the Grand Qur'an (87) has no reason to look at what others have been given (88). So the commands fall out naturally: overlook graciously, crave nothing they have, grieve over no one, and be gentle with those who believe.

## Where we are: the surah ends where it began

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the frame. The surah opened with the hostility of the disbelievers of Makkah against the Holy Prophet ﷺ, along with brief words of comfort for him. Now, at the end of the surah, more words of comfort appear — to mollify his concern about their grudge and their hostility.

That is the emotional situation these four ayat address. And ayah 85 answers it by widening the lens — past Makkah and its quarrels, out to the heavens and the earth themselves.

## Ayah 85: a universe made "with the truth"

**"And We did not create the heavens and the earth and all that is between them except with the truth, and the Hour is surely coming."**

Ibn Kathir gives *bi'l-ḥaqq* — "with the truth" — a very concrete sense: **with justice**. And he immediately supplies the purpose clause from elsewhere in the Qur'an, "to requite those who do evil with that which they have done" (53:31). Truth here is not decoration. It means the world is built such that deeds receive their due.

He then sets two passages alongside it, and together they show that denying the Hour and thinking the world pointless are not two errors but one:

- **"And We did not create the heaven and the earth, and all that is between them without purpose! That is what those who disbelieve think! Then let those who disbelieve be warned of the Fire!"** (38:27)
- **"Did you think that We created you in play, and that you would not be brought back to Us?" So exalted be Allah, the Truth, the King, none has the right to be worshipped but He, the Lord of the Honored Throne!** (23:115–116)

Notice how the second passage pairs the two ideas in one breath: created *in play*, and *not brought back*. Remove the return, and the whole thing becomes a game.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the argument step by step.** Allah did not create the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them but with truth and wisdom. The wise consideration behind that creation is that people should believe in the existence of the Maker of the universe, attest to His Oneness and supremacy, and obey His injunctions. Bound up with that is the consequence of not doing so — that once Allah's argument stands established, the defaulter should be punished. But this promised punishment does not seem to come in full right here in this mortal world. Therefore it has to be somewhere else, and for that a time is fixed: the Qiyāmah, the Day of Judgment. And that Hour is sure to come. As Maʿārif puts it, everyone will be taken care of there.

This is the passage's answer to the oldest complaint in the world — *the wrongdoers are getting away with it.* They are not. The books are simply not closed yet.

## "So overlook their faults with gracious forgiveness"

Now the practical instruction, still in ayah 85. Ibn Kathir ties it directly to what precedes: Allah informed His Prophet ﷺ about the Hour, and that it will be the faults of the idolaters when they insult him and reject the message he brings them. That is where those accounts will be settled. So the command to overlook is not "this does not matter." It is "**this is not yours to settle.**"

Ibn Kathir places beside it an ayah carrying the same instruction: **"So turn away from them, and say: 'Salām (Peace!)'. But they will come to know"** (43:89). The last clause is the point — the turning away is not resignation; it rests on a certainty about what is coming.

**What makes the overlooking "gracious"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives a two-part definition that is worth memorising: to overlook their wicked behaviour in a gracious manner means **neither to pay attention to their behaviour nor to complain about it**. Not brooding on it in private, and not rehearsing the grievance in public. A forgiveness with no reproach attached to it.

**A note the scholars add.** Mujahid, Qatadah and others said of this command: "This was before fighting was prescribed." Ibn Kathir agrees with them, and gives the reason: this surah was revealed in Makkah, and fighting was prescribed after the Hijrah. They are identifying the stage of revelation at which this instruction was given.

## Ayah 86: why *these* two names

**"Verily, your Lord is *al-Khallāq al-ʿAlīm*"** — rendered by Ibn Kathir as "Verily, your Lord is the Knowing Creator," and elsewhere as "Surely your Lord is the Master Creator, All-Knowing."

Ibn Kathir reads this ayah as **a confirmation of the Day of Resurrection** and of Allah's power — may He be exalted — to bring the Hour to pass. He then unpacks the two names in two short sentences, and each one answers an objection a denier raises about being raised again:

- *Can He?* — **He is the Creator, and nothing is beyond Him.**
- *Could He even find us?* — **He is the Knowing, Who knows what has been dispersed from people's bodies and scattered throughout the regions of the earth.**

Ibn Kathir cites the passage where the Qur'an makes the same two moves in sequence: **"Is not He, Who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them? Yes, indeed! He is the Knowing, Creator. Verily, His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, 'Be!' — and it is! So glorified and exalted is He above all that they associate with Him, and in whose Hands is the dominion of all things, and to Him you shall return"** (36:81–83).

**And then the personal turn.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notices that these same two names are pointed straight at the Prophet's ﷺ own situation: his Lord is great as Creator and great as the Master Knower as well. He knows his patience and fortitude, and He knows the evil machinations of his enemies too. Therefore He is to exact from them the full return of what they have been doing.

So *al-ʿAlīm* — the Knowing — is at once cosmic and intimate here. He knows what has been scattered from a body across the regions of the earth; He also knows a servant's patience and exactly what it cost. Note too that the ayah says **"your Lord"** — *rabbuka* in the Arabic. The address is personal, not abstract.

## Ayah 87: "the seven of the *mathānī* and the Grand Qur'an"

**"And indeed, We have bestowed upon you seven of the *mathānī*, and the Grand Qur'an."**

Ibn Kathir reports that there were some differences among the scholars over the meaning of "seven of the *mathānī*", and he gives both positions with their authorities.

**First view — the seven long surahs.** Held by Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and others: they are al-Baqarah, Āl ʿImrān, an-Nisā', al-Mā'idah, al-Anʿām, al-Aʿrāf and Yūnus. Saʿīd bin Jubayr said of them: "In them, Allah explains the obligations, the Ḥudūd (legal limits), stories and rulings." Ibn ʿAbbās said: "He explains the parables, stories and lessons."

**Second view — Sūrat al-Fātiḥah,** which is composed of seven ayat. This was reported from ʿAlī, ʿUmar, Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "The *Bismillāh* is completing seven Ayah, which Allah has given exclusively to you [Muslims]." It is also the opinion of Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī, ʿAbdullāh bin ʿUmayr, Ibn Abī Mulaykah, Shahr bin Ḥawshab, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Mujāhid.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that most commentators take the seven oft-repeated verses to be al-Fātiḥah — because its seven verses are repeated in every Ṣalāh, which is precisely why they are called *oft-repeated* — and that on this reading the words "and the glorious Qur'an" that follow are of an explanatory nature, referring to the same seven verses rather than to a second thing.

### From the Sunnah

**Al-Bukhari recorded two hadiths on this topic.** The first is from Abū Saʿīd bin al-Muʿallā, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ passed by me while I was praying. He called out for me but I did not come until I finished my prayer. Then I came to him, and he asked, *'What stopped you from coming to me?'* I said, 'I was praying.' He said, *'Did not Allah say: "O you who believe! Answer Allah (by obeying Him) and (His) Messenger when he calls you…?"'* (8:24) *'Shall I not teach you the most magnificent Surah before I leave the Masjid?'* Then the Prophet ﷺ went to leave the Masjid, and I reminded him, so he said, *'Al-Ḥamdu lillāhi Rabbi'l-ʿālamīn* — All praises and thanks be to Allah, the Lord of all that exists (1:2) — *this is the seven of the Mathānī and the Qur'an which I have been given.'*"

The second was reported from Abū Hurayrah, who said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Umm al-Qur'ān* — the Mother, or the Essence, of the Qur'an — *is the seven Mathānī and the Grand Qur'an."*

**Ibn Kathir's reconciliation** is a small lesson in how to hold two reports together. This means al-Fātiḥah is the seven *mathānī* and the Grand Qur'an — but this does not contradict the statement that the seven *mathānī* are the seven long surahs, because they too share these attributes, as does the whole Qur'an. He points to Allah's words: **"Allah has sent down the best statement, a Book, its parts resembling each other in goodness and truth, oft-recited"** (39:23). So, as Ibn Kathir puts it, it is oft-recited in one way, and its parts resemble one another in another way — and this too is the Grand Qur'an.

### Al-Fātiḥah as the whole Qur'an in miniature

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what it means that Sūrat al-Fātiḥah has been called the Glorious Qur'an in this ayah: it indicates that al-Fātiḥah is, in a way, the whole Qur'an — **because the basic principles of Islam have been merged into it.** Seven short verses you already recite in every prayer carry, in compressed form, what the rest of the Book unfolds at length.

## Ayah 88: eyes that do not stretch, and a wing that lowers

**"Look not with your eyes ambitiously at what We have given to certain classes of them, nor grieve over them. And lower your wings to the believers."**

The hinge of the whole passage is the connection between 87 and 88, and Ibn Kathir states it plainly. Allah is saying to His Prophet ﷺ: *Since We have given you the Grand Qur'an, then do not look at this world and its attractions, or the transient delights that We have given to its people* — **in order to test them.** That last phrase reframes everything. What has been handed to them is not a prize awarded; it is an examination set.

Three separate commands sit in this ayah.

**1. "Look not with your eyes ambitiously."** The command is about looking — the lingering, longing glance. Ibn Kathir cites the identical wording elsewhere (20:131) and glosses it: **be content with the Grand Qur'an that Allah has given to you, and do not long for the luxuries and transient delights that they have.** Al-ʿAwfī reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said of this: "He [in this Ayah] forbade a man to wish for what his companion has." And on "certain classes of them," Mujāhid said: "This refers to the rich."

**2. "Nor grieve over them."** Ibn Kathir: do not envy what they have in this world, and **do not upset yourself with regret for their rejection of you and their opposition to your religion.** Two very different griefs are being lifted here — the ache of not having what they have, and the ache of not reaching them. Both are set down.

**3. "And lower your wings to the believers."** The words picture a wing being lowered; Ibn Kathir's gloss is simply **be gentle with them.** He brings the parallel command, "And lower your wings to the believers who follow you" (26:215), and then the description of the Prophet ﷺ himself: **"Verily, there has come unto you a Messenger from among yourselves. It grieves him that you should receive any injury or difficulty. He is anxious for you, for the believers — he is full of pity, kind and merciful"** (9:128).

The sequence is worth sitting with. Attention that is not spent envying and not spent grieving is attention left over for the people who are actually with you.

## Living it

Read as one instruction, these four ayat ask for four things:

- **Trust the accounting.** Because the heavens and the earth were made with truth, no injustice done to you is lost. Ibn Kathir's reading of *bi'l-ḥaqq* as *justice* means the demand for fairness is answered by the design of the universe itself — just not on your timetable.
- **Forgive without residue.** Maʿārif's definition is the test: neither pay attention to it, nor complain about it. If you are still narrating the offence, the overlooking is not yet gracious.
- **Measure your wealth by what you were given.** The Prophet ﷺ was told to be content with the Grand Qur'an and not long for the luxuries and transient delights of those Mujāhid identified as "the rich." Ibn ʿAbbās's gloss — a man is forbidden to wish for what his companion has — puts that same scale in every hand.
- **Spend your softness on the believers.** Whatever hardness the opposition provokes, the ayah routes it away from the people around you. Be gentle with them, as Ibn Kathir says — after the model of the Messenger ﷺ who was "full of pity, kind and merciful."

passages.title: The clear warner and those who cut Scripture apart
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** The Prophet ﷺ is told to state plainly who he is — a clear warner (ayah 89) — and then Allah turns to the people who had organised themselves against that warning: the *muqtasimūn*, the pact-makers and oath-swearers, who took the revealed Book and cut it into pieces, believing in some of it and rejecting the rest (ayat 90–91). The unit closes with an oath from Allah Himself that every one of them will be questioned about everything they used to do (ayat 92–93). What holds the five ayat together is a single line of thought: **a clear warning has been delivered; men have handled it by fragmenting it; and no fragment of their handling will escape the reckoning.**

## "Say: I am the plain warner" (ayah 89)

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah commanded His Prophet ﷺ to tell the people, *"I am indeed a plain warner"* — meaning one who has come to warn them of a severe punishment they will suffer if they reject him, as happened to those nations before them who disbelieved in their Messengers, upon whom Allah sent His punishment and His vengeance.

So the threat is not something newly invented for Quraysh. It is the standing pattern of how Allah has dealt with a people who were warned clearly and rejected the Messenger sent to them.

Ayah 90 follows with a comparison. Ibn Kathir's rendering reads, *"As We have sent down on the Muqtasimin (conspiring confederates)"*; the translation supplied here reads it as a warning similar to what was sent to those who divided the Scripture. Either way, what is coming to the people addressed now is set alongside what came to an earlier set of people — and Ibn Kathir moves straight on to explain who those *muqtasimīn* were.

**The parable of the naked warner.** Ibn Kathir brings a hadith that makes the image vivid — reported **in the two Sahihs from Abu Musa**, that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> The parable of myself and that with which Allah has sent me is that of a man who came to his people and said, "O people! I have seen the army with my own eyes, and I am a naked warner, so escape, escape!" Some of his people obeyed him and set out at nightfall, setting off at a slow pace and managing to escape. Others did not believe him and stayed where they were until the next morning, when the army overtook them and destroyed them, wiping them out. This is the parable of the one who obeys me and follows what I have brought, and the example of the one who disobeys me and rejects the truth that I have brought.

Notice what the parable establishes. First, the warner has *seen* what is coming — "with my own eyes"; he is not guessing. Second, the warning is shouted, not murmured: "escape, escape!" Third, the two groups face the identical danger and hear the identical words; what separates the saved from the destroyed is nothing but whether they moved. And those who were saved were not the fastest — they "set out at nightfall, setting off at a slow pace." Slow obedience saved them. Staying put destroyed the others.

## The *muqtasimūn*: people who made denial into an oath (ayah 90)

Ibn Kathir says *al-muqtasimīn* refers to **those who had made a pact to oppose, deny, and insult the Prophets.** He then does something worth following closely: he establishes the sense of the word by lining up the places in the Qur'an where the same verb of oath-swearing appears in the mouths of rejectors.

- Of the people of Sālih: *"They said, 'Swear to one another by Allah that we shall make a secret night attack on him and his household'"* (27:49) — that is, they plotted to kill him at night. **Mujahid** said that *taqāsamū* here means "they swore an oath."
- *"And they swear by Allah with their strongest oaths, that Allah will not raise up one who dies"* (16:38).
- *"Did you not before swear that you would not leave the world for the Hereafter?"* (14:44).
- *"Are they those of whom you swore that Allah would never show them mercy?"* (7:49).

Ibn Kathir's conclusion is striking: **"It is as if they took an oath for every single thing that they denied in this world, so they are called the *muqtasimīn*."**

Sit with that portrait. These are not people with honest doubts. Every denial is sworn to. They make their rejection a binding position, a group commitment, something they have staked their word on in front of others — which is precisely what makes retreat from it so hard. Faith is difficult for a man who has publicly sworn that he is right. And because these are oaths people swear *to one another*, the word carries the flavour of conspiracy — Ibn Kathir's own rendering of ayah 90 calls them "conspiring confederates," people bound by a pact: a shared, negotiated, agreed-upon unbelief rather than an individual's confusion.

## Making the Book into pieces (ayah 91)

The word rendered "parts" is *ʿiḍīn*. The classical commentators record two readings of who is meant, and both are preserved in Ibn Kathir; where scholars genuinely differed it is better to hold both than to flatten one.

**First view: the People of the Book.** Ibn Kathir's own gloss is that "they have split up the Books that were revealed to them, believing in parts of them and rejecting parts of them." **Al-Bukhari reported that Ibn ʿAbbās** said of *"who have made the Qur'an into parts"*: "They are the People of the Book, who divided the Book into parts, believing in some of it, and rejecting some of it."

**Second view: the Quraysh.** Some said that the *muqtasimīn* are the Quraysh, that "the Qur'an" here means this Qur'an rather than the earlier Scriptures, and that "made it into parts" refers to what **ʿAtā'** said — that some of them said the Prophet ﷺ was a sorcerer, some said he was crazy, some a soothsayer. These various allegations were the parts: one revelation carved up into a menu of slanders. Ibn Kathir notes this opinion was also reported from **Ad-Daḥḥāk** and others.

Both readings describe the same disease showing up in two communities. The Scripture arrives as one whole and is received as an assortment — some of it kept, some discarded, some relabelled — with the person doing the sorting, not the Book, sitting in the seat of judgement.

## An episode behind the second reading: al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra's committee

Ibn Kathir supplies a concrete scene for the Quraysh reading. **Muhammad ibn Ishāq reported from Ibn ʿAbbās** that al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra — a man holding a noble position among his people — rallied a group of Quraysh behind him when *al-Mawsim* had come, the time for pilgrims to meet in Makkah for Hajj.

He said to them: "O people of Quraysh! The time of al-Mawsim has come, and delegations of Arabs will come to you during this time. They will have heard some things about this companion of yours" — meaning the Prophet ﷺ — "so agree on one opinion, let there be no contradicting or denials of each other's sayings."

They said: "And you, O Abū ʿAbd Shams, give us an opinion and we will say that." He said: "No, you make the suggestions and I will listen."

They said, "We say he is a soothsayer." He said, "He is not a soothsayer."
They said, "We say he is crazy." He said, "He is not crazy."
They said, "We say he is a poet." He said, "He is not a poet."
They said, "We say he is a sorcerer." He said, "He is not a sorcerer."

"So what should we say?"

He said: "By Allah, what he says is as palatable as something sweet, so you cannot say anything against it without it being obviously false. Therefore the most appropriate thing you can say is that he is a sorcerer."

They left having agreed upon that, and Allah revealed concerning them: *"who have made the Qur'an into parts."*

Read that exchange slowly, because it is a confession dressed as a strategy meeting. A man of standing in Makkah examines every available slander in turn and rules each one out — by his own admission the Qur'an is not the speech of a soothsayer, not the raving of a madman, not the craft of a poet. He even testifies to its sweetness and admits that any charge against it will be obviously false. And then he selects the least indefensible lie and sends the committee out with it. On this reading, that is what "making the Qur'an into parts" looked like on the ground: a coordinated line agreed in advance so that the arriving delegations would hear one story.

Ibn Kathir adds that "into parts" here means "of different types" — and that it was this group who received the answer of ayat 92–93: *"So, by your Lord, We shall certainly call all of them to account, for all that they used to do."* Those, he says, were the group who said that about the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The committee's agreed line will be reviewed at a session they did not schedule.

## "So by your Lord, We will certainly question them all" (ayat 92–93)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that in ayah 92 Allah has sworn **by His own sacred Being**, declaring that all such people — those who came earlier and those who came later — shall definitely be questioned. The oath is worded *"by your Lord"*, spoken to the Prophet ﷺ: the same Lord who has just told him to say "I am the plain warner" is the one guaranteeing that the warning has teeth.

**What will they be asked about?** The sources give complementary answers.

- **Abū al-ʿĀliya** — reported by Abū Jaʿfar from ar-Rabīʿ — said: "All the people will be asked about two things on the Day of Resurrection: what they used to worship, and what their response was to the Messengers." Which is exactly the two-part shape of this passage: a Messenger came clearly (ayah 89), and a people replied with organised rejection (ayat 90–91).
- Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that the Companions asked the Prophet ﷺ what the questioning would be about, and he said it would be about saying *lā ilāha illā Allāh* — "there is no god worthy of worship but Allah." Al-Qurtubi, after reporting this narration in his Tafsir, explains that it means **fulfilling this pledge practically**, as the Kalimah signifies — not a bare verbal statement, since verbal attestation was made by the hypocrites too.

**A note on ayah 93 and 55:39.** ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalha reported that Ibn ʿAbbās recited *"So, by your Lord, We shall certainly call all of them to account for all that they used to do"* and then recited *"So on that Day no question will be asked of man or jinn as to his sin"* (55:39), and explained: they will not be asked, "Did you do such and such?" — because Allah knows that better than they do. Rather He will say, **"Why did you do such and such?"**

That single clarification changes the mood of the whole passage. The questioning is not an investigation; nothing is being discovered. It is the demand for a reason.

## Living it

**Faith is not a slogan you hold; it is a claim you honour.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers the practical fruit of ayat 92–93 here. A simple verbal statement is not what is desired, because verbal attestation is exactly what the hypocrites offered. **Al-Hasan al-Basri** said: faith does not become a living reality by taking on a particular style and form, and the religion does not prosper by simply having the best of wishes for it — **"īmān is the name of that certitude which has been poured into the heart and which has been proved true by deeds."**

Maʿārif illustrates this with a report it cites through al-Qurtubi, from Zayd ibn Arqam, that the Prophet ﷺ said that a person who says *lā ilāha illā Allāh* — "there is no god worthy of worship but Allah" — with *ikhlāṣ*, totally unalloyed sincerity, will definitely go to Jannah. When the people asked him how *ikhlāṣ* relates to this Kalimah, he said: **when this Kalimah stops a person from what Allah has prohibited as unlawful, then it is with *ikhlāṣ*.** That is a usable test. The measure of your declaration is not how it sounds; it is what it stops you from doing.

**Do not become a private muqtasim.** The condemnation in ayah 91 lands on people who received a whole Book and treated it as a tray to pick from. That instinct did not die with the generations named here. Any believer who embraces the verses that flatter his habits and quietly sets aside the ones that would cost him something is doing, on a small scale, what Ibn ʿAbbās described: dividing the Book into parts, believing in some of it and rejecting some of it.

**Beware of denial that has hardened into a position.** What made the *muqtasimūn* immovable was not evidence but commitment — oaths sworn, opinions agreed, a line to hold in front of others. Al-Walīd could see clearly enough to rule out every slander, and still would not say so. The lesson is to keep your account with Allah free from the sunk cost of your own public statements, so that when the truth is shown to you, you are still able to move — even at nightfall, even at a slow pace, like the people in the parable who survived.

passages.title: Proclaim openly; worship until the certainty comes
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat close Sūrat al-Ḥijr, and they read as one continuous instruction to the Prophet ﷺ at a hinge moment in his mission: go public with the message, do not let the idolaters deflect you, and when their words press on your chest, take shelter in prayer — and keep worshipping until death comes. The passage moves steadily inward: an outward command (94), Allah's guarantee against the enemy (95–96), the inner wound that the insults leave (97), and the cure for it (98–99).

## When the message stepped into daylight (94–95)

This is one of those places where knowing *when* an ayah came down unlocks it entirely.

Ibn Kathir records, from Abu ʿUbaydah reporting from ʿAbdullah bin Masʿud: "The Prophet ﷺ was still practising and preaching Islam secretly until this Ayah was revealed — *fa-ṣdaʿ bimā tuʾmar* — then he and his Companions came out into the open."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the picture. Before ayah 94, the Prophet ﷺ and his noble Companions used to pray and recite the Qur'an secretly, lest they be seen and harmed. The work of passing the message on, of teaching and training, was also kept secret and limited to a counted few — because doing it openly would have handed the disbelievers the opportunity to bring harm on them. "Therefore," says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, "from that time onwards, the mission was pursued openly and publicly in all its aspects, recitation of the Qur'an, acts of worship, the call, the propagation, everything."

So ayah 94 is the ayah that ended the private phase of Islam. Prayer that had been hidden, recitation that had been muffled, teaching confined to a trusted few — all of it stepped out into daylight on the strength of this one command.

And notice what makes it possible. The command comes in 94; the protection is promised in 95. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it plainly: in this verse Allah Himself has taken the responsibility of seeing that they stay safe from those who deride their faith and bring harm to them. The Prophet ﷺ was not told to step into the open and hope. He was told to step into the open because Allah had already guaranteed the outcome.

As for the command itself — **فَٱصْدَعْ بِمَا تُؤْمَرُ**, "So proclaim what you have been commanded" — Ibn ʿAbbas glossed it with startling simplicity: it means "Go ahead with it." Ibn Kathir adds that according to another report it means *ifʿal mā tuʾmar*, "do what you are commanded." And Mujahid gave a concrete reading: it is reciting the Qur'an aloud during prayer — which lands exactly where the secrecy had been, since recitation was among the things that had been kept quiet.

That second wording is worth pausing on. "Do what you are *commanded*" — the content of the proclamation is not the caller's to choose or soften. That becomes the whole point of the next phrase.

## "Turn away" is not retreat (94–96)

The second half of ayah 94 — "and turn away from the idolaters" — is not a command to abandon calling them. The same ayah has just ordered open proclamation *to* them.

Ibn Kathir's gloss makes the sense clear: convey what has been revealed to you by your Lord, "and do not pay attention to the idolators who want to turn you away from the signs of Allah." He then cites the verse that names their real hope: *"They wish that you should compromise for them, so that they would compromise for you"* (68:9).

So "turn away" means: do not negotiate the message. Do not trade a piece of it for peace. Their mockery, their offers, their pressure — none of it gets a hearing when the question is what Allah has revealed.

And do not fear them, Ibn Kathir continues, because Allah will suffice you against them and will protect you from them. He puts this ayah beside the later verse: *"O Messenger! Proclaim that which has been revealed to you from your Lord. And if you do not do it, then you have not conveyed His Message. Allah will protect you from mankind"* (5:67) — the same pairing of an uncompromising command with an unbreakable guarantee.

Ayah 96 then tells us who these men actually were. Not simply cruel — they were those "who set up other gods with Allah." The mockery was the surface; setting up rivals to Allah was the substance. Ibn Kathir calls this ayah "a strong warning and grave threat against those who have other deities along with Allah." And the warning itself is left open: *fasawfa yaʿlamūn*, "they will soon come to know." Nothing is specified, which makes the threat heavier rather than lighter.

## The five, and who dealt with them (95)

**إِنَّا كَفَيْنَٰكَ ٱلْمُسْتَهْزِءِينَ** — "Surely We will be sufficient for you against the mockers."

Ibn Kathir cites Muhammad bin Ishaq: the great ones among the mockers were five men, elders and noblemen among their people — al-Aswad bin al-Muttalib Abu Zamʿah of Banu Asad; al-Aswad bin ʿAbd Yaghuth of Banu Zahrah; al-Walid bin al-Mughirah of Banu Makhzum; al-ʿAs bin Waʾil of Banu Sahm; and al-Harith bin al-Talatilah of Khuzaʿah. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same five, naming the last as Harith ibn Talhah.) Ibn Ishaq adds, with the qualification "according to what I heard," that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had supplicated against al-Aswad bin al-Muttalib because of the pain and mockery he had suffered at his hands: *"O Allah, make him blind and take the life of his son."* When their evil went to extremes and their mockery of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went too far, Allah revealed these ayat.

Ibn Kathir then records the sequel from Ibn Ishaq, who had it from Yazid bin Ruman, from ʿUrwah bin al-Zubayr or one of the other scholars. Jibril came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he was making *ṭawāf* — circling the Kaʿbah in worship — and stood there, with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ standing next to him. Al-Aswad bin al-Muttalib passed by; Jibril threw a green leaf in his face, and he went blind. Al-Aswad bin ʿAbd Yaghuth passed; Jibril pointed to his stomach, which swelled up, and he died. Al-Walid bin al-Mughirah passed; Jibril pointed at an old wound low on his ankle — a trivial scratch from an arrow that had caught in his trailing garment two years earlier — and it opened again and killed him. Al-ʿAs bin Waʾil passed; Jibril pointed to the instep of his foot; he set off on his donkey for al-Taʾif, rested by a thorn tree, and a thorn pierced that foot and killed him. Al-Harith bin al-Talatilah passed; Jibril pointed at his head, it filled with pus, and he died. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān summarises the episode the same way: the five were brought down miraculously at Jibril's signal.

The shape of the promise is worth noticing. Allah did not say "We will help you against them." He said *We* will be sufficient for you against them — and in the account Ibn Ishaq relates, the Prophet ﷺ simply stood beside Jibril while it happened. His instruction in 94 was only ever to proclaim and to look past them; the dealing-with was Allah's own undertaking.

## The wound named, then the cure prescribed (97–98)

**وَلَقَدْ نَعْلَمُ أَنَّكَ يَضِيقُ صَدْرُكَ بِمَا يَقُولُونَ** — "Indeed, We know that your breast becomes tight because of what they say."

Before Allah prescribes anything, He acknowledges. He does not open by telling His Messenger ﷺ not to feel it. He opens by saying that He knows he feels it — that the constant abuse constricted his chest. The pain is named by the very One who is about to address it.

Ibn Kathir renders the sense of 97–98 as a single address: "We know, O Muhammad, that you are distressed by their insults towards you, but do not let that weaken your resolve or cause you to give up conveying the Message of Allah. Put your trust in Him, for He will suffice you and will support you against them. Keep yourself busy with remembering Allah, praising Him, glorifying Him, and worshipping Him."

Note how much is conceded and how little is excused. The pain is real and named; it is simply not permitted to become a reason to stop.

Then the prescription: **فَسَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ وَكُن مِّنَ ٱلسَّٰجِدِينَ** — "So glorify the praises of your Lord and be of those who prostrate themselves."

*Tasbīḥ* is glorifying Allah; *ḥamd* is praising Him. Ibn Kathir's gloss gathers them with two more — "remembering Allah, praising Him, glorifying Him, and worshipping Him" — and he specifies that this last means Ṣalāh, the formal prayer. So the prescription is not a mood but an act you can perform. Where the mockers debase, the servant exalts.

The phrasing of the second half repays attention: not "prostrate," but "be *of* those who prostrate." It asks for belonging to a company, a settled identity, not a single act.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the practical rule out of ayat 97 and 98 under the heading *The Spiritual Defence Against Enemy Hostility*: when a person faces heart-rending words and deeds from enemies and is bothered by the anxiety they cause, there is a spiritual cure — let him or her get busy with *tasbīḥ* and *ʿibādah* (worship), praising Allah and praying before Him, and Allah will Himself remove that pain and anxiety.

Ibn Kathir places a hadith here. Imam Ahmad reported from Nuʿaym bin Hammar that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say that Allah said: *"O son of Adam! It is not too difficult for you to perform four Rakʿat at the beginning of the day; if you do them, I will take care of you until the end of it."* Four rakʿat — four units of prayer — set against a whole day. The remedy comes with a promise attached: give Allah the opening of your day, and He undertakes the rest of it.

## The term of worship: until al-yaqīn (99)

**وَٱعْبُدْ رَبَّكَ حَتَّىٰ يَأْتِيَكَ ٱلْيَقِينُ** — "and worship your Lord until *al-yaqīn* comes to you."

*Al-yaqīn* means "the certainty," and Ibn Kathir gathers the reports that say what certainty is meant. Al-Bukhari reported that Salim said it means death; Ibn Kathir identifies this Salim as Salim bin ʿAbdullah bin ʿUmar, and notes that Ibn Jarir also recorded the same explanation from him.

The word is confirmed by the Prophet's ﷺ own usage. Ibn Kathir cites a report in the Sahih from Umm al-ʿAlaʾ, one of the women of the Ansar. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came in to ʿUthman bin Mazʿun after his death, she said, "May the mercy of Allah be upon you, Abu al-Saʾib. My testimony over you is that Allah has honoured you." He ﷺ said, *"How do you know that Allah has honoured him?"* She said, "May my father and mother be sacrificed for you, O Messenger of Allah! If not him, then who else?" He ﷺ said — and the Arabic in Ibn Kathir's text has *jāʾahu al-yaqīn* — *"As far as he is concerned, the death has come to him, and I hope for good for him."* The very word the ayah uses is the word the Prophet ﷺ used for what had arrived for a man who had died.

So the last words of the sūrah set the term of worship, and the term is a lifetime. Ibn Kathir draws the ruling: acts of worship such as prayer are obligatory upon a person for as long as his mind is sound, and he should pray according to his best ability. He cites Sahih al-Bukhari, from ʿImran bin Husayn, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Pray standing, and if you cannot, then sitting, and if you cannot, then on your side."* Inability reduces the form of the prayer; it does not cancel it. The only thing that ends the obligation is death.

## The error the closing ayah rules out

Ibn Kathir is emphatic that it is a mistake to read *al-yaqīn* as *maʿrifah* — "spiritual knowing" — as some of the Sufis do, holding that once a person attains that level he is free of these obligations. Ibn Kathir calls that "disbelief, misguidance and ignorance."

His argument is not merely an assertion, and it is worth following. The Prophets, peace be upon them, and their companions were the most knowledgeable of all people about Allah — about His rights, His attributes, and the glorification He deserves. Yet at the same time they were the people who worshipped Him the most, continuing in good deeds until the time they died. The ones who knew Allah best were the ones who worshipped Him most; knowledge of Him never released anyone from serving Him.

## Living it

Read as one piece, these six ayat give a believer a complete posture under pressure.

**Say what Allah has commanded, and do not trim it.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a careful rule from this episode for anyone engaged in *tablīgh* and *daʿwah* — conveying the message and calling others to Allah. Where a worker in the way of Allah sees no good coming from saying what is true and right openly, and fears harm in doing so, working secretly is also correct and permissible — that is exactly what the Prophet ﷺ himself did until ayah 94 came down. But when the option and the ability exist to proclaim things openly, no delay should be made in taking a public stance. Discretion is a stage, not a permanent policy.

**Let the mockery be Allah's business.** He said "We will suffice you," and in Ibn Ishaq's account the five were dealt with while the Prophet ﷺ stood beside Jibril.

**When the words get in, pray.** The remedy Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws from ayat 97–98 is *tasbīḥ* and worship — praising Allah and praying before Him; the ayah's own words add *sujūd*, prostration, and belonging to the company of those who prostrate. And the report from Imam Ahmad attaches a promise to four rakʿat at the start of the day: Allah's care for the rest of it.

**Do not set a finishing line.** The one deadline given for worship is *al-yaqīn*, and it is not a spiritual rank you graduate to. It is death.

Ibn Kathir ends his commentary on the sūrah with the words that its last ayah invites: "To Allah be praise and thanks. Praise be to Allah for His guidance. It is to Him that we turn for help and it is in Him that we put our trust."
